Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

Mr. Chairman. When the Committee rose at one o'clock I was referring to clause 11 of the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company add I had pointed out that a similar clause to that clause 11 had existed in the general Railway Act of the Dominion and that iin the discussions upon the Railway Commission Bill the clause, then No. 59, I think it was, in Bill No. 21, was struck out because it was conceded on the part of the government that the clause was an objectionable one and ought mot to be in the Bill. We find the same clause, 59, in the general Act, inserted in the private Bill of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and not only containing all the provisions that were then in the old section of the general Railway Act but very material additions made to it. I was saying that it appeared to me that the insertion of clause 11 in this charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the additions made to the old clause bore evidence that the object of inserting it was to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to give to the Grand Trunk Railway Company the $25,000,000 of common stock practically without any payment for it; at all events, merely for the concession of some rights, powers and privileges, and I was pointing Mr. BARKER.
out that it was impossible for any person to value these rights, powers and privileges, that the two companies set their own value upon them and make that value an excuse for the granting of the whole $25,000,000 of common stock. At present I will not say one word as to the broad question whether it is right that such a thing should be permitted at all. I only point out that in this agreement bonds are authorized sufficient in amount to construct the whole railway, that three-quarters of these bonds are to be guaranteed by the government and the remaining one-quarter by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Therefore, the construction of the railway is provided for out of the bonds. Preferred stock amounting to $20,000,000 is authorized, and I presume- and I think it is a fair inference-that the $20,000,000 in preferred stock is to meet the expenditure necessary to provide the equipment of $15,000,000 on the western section and $5,000,000 on the eastern section. After you have built the railway and equipped it, what then is needed of the $25,000,000 of common stock ? It seems to me that a consideration of these figures and the fact of the bonds being sufficient to build the railway and the preferred stock being sufficient to equip the railway give us further indication, if any were needed, that the $25,000,000 of common stock is to be placed upon this company without one dollar in respect of it entering into the treasury of the company. The result will be, as has been pointed out more than once in this House, that the railway will have to bear the burden in the shape of dividends upon that $25,000,000 without any corresponding advantage from it. I think, that, while there may be some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who are prepared to go the length of saying that the stock ought to be authorized to be issued whether paid for or not, there is not a gentleman representing Manitoba or the North-west Territories who will agree to support any such proposition. We have heard a good deal on this subject and I should expect that every hon. gentleman representing the North-west Territories would stand up in favour of any proposition requiring that every dollar of the stock should be paid for in cash. Whether these hon. gentlemen will do so or not I cannot say. Why should the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, practically the same company-the directors of the Grand Trunk Railway are the people entering into this agreement on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific-be enabled to sit down and enter into an arrangement by which one shall give to the other, exchanging from the right hand to the left, $25,000,000 of stock upon a mere bargain about privileges that they estimate the value of and the country have no voice in it ? Surely this is wrong. Surely there is no need for it. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway

Company want to make traffic arrangements with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, arrangements for terminals, arrangements for elevators, for docks, for shipping facilities, surely these are matters of mutual convenience that they can agree upon one with the other. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company must'be of enormous advantage to the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada just as possibly the connection with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada will be an advantage to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. This is a matter of mutual convenience and should be the subject of mutual [DOT] bargain, not a matter for $25,000,000 of stock to be ranked as paid up stock being handed from the one to the other. That is the point 1 make and I do not think it can be too strongly pressed upon this country. We have heard time and again denunciations of the practice of watering stock. What more barefaced watering of stock could there be than that' which is provided for by this arrangement ? There is an enormous provision for it-$25,000,000 of money on the books without a dollar in fact. Surely that has only fo be mentioned to shock the people. It is not fair when we take into account the effect ijiat the overloading of the company with stock that does not represent cash will have upon the farmers and shippers of the country. It is useless to say that it means nothing. When the question of rates comes up that stock will have to stand as stock bearing dividends and the rates that are to be authorized by the railway commissioners will have to be sufficient to enable reasonable dividends to be paid upon that stock. These commissioners will have to treat that stock on the same footing as if a hundred cents on the dollar had been paid in cash for it. They will have no authority to distinguish between one class of stock and another. On the face of the books as authorized by an Act of parliament they have so much paid up stock and whether paid in cash or paid by the writing of a signature makes no difference to them. They will have no right to distinguish and the result will be that the rates to be imposed upon the people of this country in respect to that stock will be precisely the same as if $25,000,000 in hard cash had been paid by the company upon it. I desire for that reason to impose upon those who subscribe to that $25,000,000 the obligation that applies to every man who takes $100 in any company-that he shall be subject to any calls until that $100 is paid up. So, I say that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or any other company subscribing for this $25,000,000 of common stock, should, be liable to pay $25,000,000 when called upon to do so as required by the Railway Act. I do not propose at present to occupy further time. I shall be very glad to hear from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House
what they have to say why that course should not be pursued.
With regard to the common stock, I say it must be subscribed for and for this reason : That it is to be issued only to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, with the exception of the qualifying shares. Being issued only to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, it must be subscribed for by that company, and the ordinary subscriber is to pay for his stock to the company. I want to know whether the Grand Trunk should be relieved from that ordinary obligation. As to the preferred stock, they are under no obligation under the agreement, to acquire, or own, or hold preferred stock. Therefore I propose in that amendment to simply give them the power to subscribe for it. But, I also propose to give them what the government proposes, namely : the power to acquire stock just as they have the power to acquire bonds and other things. That means, that preferred stock held by the public ; bonds held by the public ; debentures held by the public, may be bought by the Grand Trunk at the current price of the day. But when they come to the common stock, which cannot be upon the market, they shall not have that without paying 100 cents on the dollar for it. That is manifestly in the interests of the country. Why should they be given $25,000,000 ? Does any hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House undertake to stand up and say that it will never be worth $25,000,000 ? Can they say that in ten years from now that stock may not be worth 100 cents on the dollar, and that the result of that agreement may not be, that we shall have made a straight present, a gift of $25,000,000 to these people ? Why should we do so ? Why should we not tell them :	You
may subscribe for the stock if it is your interest to control that company. If you want to be a controlling power in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and for that reason want to own the majority of that stock, subscribe for it, and take your chances of there being any necessity to call up the stock. The company control the board. It is to be presumed, under these circumstances, that not one call will be made more than is necessary for the purposes of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. If 10 per cent upon that stock will suffice for all the needs of the railway company, you may depend upon it there will never be more than 10 per cent called. If it is necessary to call it, then they will get dividends upon it. But, hon. gentlemen opposite are not satisfied with that. They are so generous to the Grand Trunk, that without their paying 1 per cent upon it, they say : You may obtain dividends upon the whole. Surely it is more reasonable to say :	We have no
objection to your obtaining a dividend upon what you pay : you will have the control yourselves to prevent an unnecessary call

being made ; if you are called upon to pay 10 per cent you will get dividends upon 10 per cent ; if the requirements of the company call for 20 per cent, you will get dividends upon 20 per cent ; but you will only get dividends, upon what you pay. That is the proposition I make, and I submit the amendment with all confidence that it ought to receive the support of gentlemen on botli sides of the House.

1 would like to ask my hon. friend, merely by way of information, if he can tell me of a single railway charter that has ever gone through this House to which lias been applied the principle for which he contends In connection with this charter ?

I cannot, for the simple reason that I have never known a case where a company was given such privileges as this by contract with the government, and in connection with that a privileged section is put in the charter of the company enabling the contracting company to obtain $25,000,000 free.

Of course, my hon. friend does not expect us to take literally what he says, when he contends that this may be given free, and that there is provision in the charter for that. If he does, then I am somewhat amazed at the view he takes of the law.
Pardon me a moment, what I mean by free is, without the payment of a dollar of cash ; simply they could agree upon terms.

I assume that my hon. friend means that the payment of the stock must be in cash, that the equivalent of cash does not count; and that the payment in any equivalent of cash is what he calls giving the stock free. Now, the general principle of law is, that stock subscribed for must be paid for in cash. That is the general principle of our Company's Act, and it is the general principle that will prevail if the new railway Bill becomes law. If that be the general principle of law, and if provision is made for an exception to that to the effect that it is possible to give paid up stock to any person in payment for land, rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials of any kind, or in consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired ; then I submit respectfully to this House that under a true construction of that statute, it would be necessary that the property given must be an equivalent to cash. I submit that that is the construction the courts would put upon it. If It is to be given in payment of the stock ; the genera] principle of the law being that it should be given in cash, then the equivalent must also be equal to cash. Irrespective of that I would like to draw the attention of the
House to this fact:	That this company
receives certain limited bonding powers ; that the bonding powers are not more than sufficient to allow the roadbed to be constructed ; that in addition to the bonding powers which they have they are authorized to issue $45,000,000, worth of stock-$20,000,000 of which must go in payment for the equipment, that they put upon the road ; because they are under the obligation to equip the road to the extent of $20,000,000. You will, therefore, have to assume that the bonds will Ire sold for the equivalent of cash, for a sum equal to their face value ; that the preferred stock will be sold for the face value of $20,000,000 in order to get the equipment, and in addition to that, then you have the $25,000,000 of common stock. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) says that that common stock is to be given away to the Grand Trunk Company. Now, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have to provide terminal facilities. Where are they going to get the money for that '! They have to build a thousand miles of branch lines, which they must equip. Where are they going to get the money to do that ? Where are they going to get the money, not only to provide the first equipment of $20,000,000, but also to provide, as they go along, an equipment equal at any time to the most modern requirements.
