The argument of the Minister of Justice is that this $25,000,000 of stock must be paid for by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, because there is no provision outside of that for the cost of terminal facilities and branch lines. I have already pointed out, that the branch lines are not covered by the general mortgage, and that the cost of branch lines, to the extent of 75 per cent at least, would, I suppose, be paid for by independent mortgages, which would be effected upon them. My hon. friend cannot get very much consolation from his argument with regard to that. I was impressed to a certain extent by the argument of the hon. Minister of Justice until the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Northrup) brought to the attention of the House the provisions of clauses 15 and 18, and it seems to me that these clauses take away from the Minister of Justice, absolutely, every shred of argument which he based upon the cost of terminal facilities. You have in clause 15, the distinct statement in so many words, that the cost of construction shall include terminal facilities. That is dealing with the eastern section, but then it is followed by clause 18, which says that the cost of construction of the western division shall include the like class of expenditure, and therefore without doubt the cost of construction of the western division does include the cost of terminal facilities. The next thing we have to examine is the bonding powers, and turning to clause 28 you find :
For the purpose of aiding the company in the construction of the western division, the government shall guarantee payment of the principal and interest of an Issue of bonds to be made by the company for a principal amount equal to 75 per centum of the cost of construction of the said divisions as defined and ascertained in accordance with the provision of paragraph IS.
Therefore, you have terminal facilities provided for to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost. If you turn to section 34, where the company is authorized to issue bonds to be guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, you find the equivalent expression, and no lawyer would have any doubt as to the meaning of that.
Inasmuch as the bonds to be guaranteed by the government only make provision for a part of the cost of construction of the western division ; the company hereby agrees that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall guarantee bonds of the company for the balance required for the construction of the said western division, exclusive of the said $20,000,000 required for first equipment.
Therefore, taking paragraphs 15, 18, 28 and 34, you have it abundantly stated, that the bond issue of the company will provide the entire cost of construction, Including the terminal facilities upon which the Minister of Justice has based his argument. At present I cannot see any answer to that. If the Minister of Justice can suggest that there is any fallacy in my reasoning with regard to this, or that I have overlooked any provision of the contract, I shall be very glad to be corrected. In view of the four clauses to which I have called attention, it does not seem to me that there can be the slightest doubt as to the accuracy of what I have stated.

While the Minister of Justice has stated the law correctly, yet, wheu it comes to a question of facts," he betrayed a lack of knowledge of the contract, and that lack of knowledge was characteristic of all the ministers who have spoken upon the subject. The amendment of the hon. member for Hamilton is to provide that proper value shall be given for $25,000,000 of common stock which is to be banded by the Grand Trunk Pacific (one part of the red-headed boy) to the Grand Trunk Railway (the other complement of the red-headed boy). The hon member (Mr. Barker) has moved his amendment for the purpose of ensuring that this railway project shall not be so loaded up with improper expenditure as to unduly increase the freight rates upon that road. In this connection we might have expected to have heard something from those redoubtable champions of the people's rights from the western country-the hon. member for Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), the hon. member for Eastern Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas), and the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver). These three gentlemen are very strenuous in their criticism of the Canadian Pacific Railway for its excessive freight rates, which they contend are due altogether to the too large, from their point of view, capitalization of that railway. Yet here we have $25,000,000 of common stock which may be given for a nominal consideration. We have the statement of the right hon. the Premier to that effect. We have had the statement of the Minister of Justice just now that this common stock will be given for its market value at the time, and that market value may be very small; it may be only five cents on the dollar ; and yet, in fixing the freight rates, it is fair to take into consideration the total amount of the capitalization of the company. In that way the company may be permitted to charge such rates as will give them a dividend on $25,000,000 of stock, which may not have brought more than $2,500,000 in the market. That is what we want to guard against. The hon. Minister of Justice said that the amount paid for the stock should be equivalent to cash. Well, that is true ; but who is to fix the value of the thing given ? Un-

der the contract, the stock may be given for rights, privileges and powers granted by the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific. As has been pointed out, these words are broad enough to include the assistance which the Grand Trunk gives in floating, the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific ; and who is to fix the value of the credit which the Grand Trunk gives to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ? There is the whole point; you have no two corporations, but you have oue corporation dealing with itself. That is the danger which we have to guard against. It is a danger which has never occurred in connection with any other contract of any other railway charter ; because there has been no other case in the same circumstances as this, where you are dealing with two parties who are really one party. It seems to me that is the crux of the whole thing. In the interest of the people who are to be accommodated by this road, it is absolutely necessary to guard against that possibility; and the only way we can guard against it is by providing that this stock shall not be given at its market value, but that its equivalent shall be paid in cash at che par value. The bon. Minister of Justice challenged the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) to show where there was any authority given to issue bonds at all. If the hon. gentleman will read clauses 29, 30 and 31 of the contract, he will see full provision there made for the issue of these bonds, their denominations, and the rate of interest they shall bear. It seems to me, as I said before, that all those gentlemen from the west who have been finding so much fault'with the excessive rates charged on the Canadian Pacific Railway, should be with us in championing the cause of the people on this occasion. Only a day or two ago the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), in a letter to the Toronto ' News,' said :
A total debt of $10,-184,653 was placed upon 550 miles of road, whose total cost was only $6,283,162, leaving the settlers to pay rates to meet six per cent Interest upon an excess sum of $4,201,491 which did not go into the roads at all. The necessary freight rates under the conditions imposed simply drove settlers out of the country.
Now, history often repeats itself, and it may be so in this case if the hon. gentlemen does not rise in his place and endeavour to prevent the government doing the very thing that was done before. If it applied in the case of the railway which the hon. gentlemen was then referring to, surely it will apply to the railway projected by the Bill before the House. Therefore, I am surprised that we have not heard from the hon. member for West Assiniboia in respect to this matter.

My hon. friend's fear is that this stock, issued at a low figure, and falling into the hands of Mr. FOWLER.
the public, will afterwards be taken into account when the question of freight rates will be considered. My hon. friend has overlooked the fact that the $25,000,000 of common stock under the contract is to pass Into the hands of the Grand Trunk Company, and will not be dealt with on the same principle as it would be if it had passed into the hands of the general public. That company will have to take this stock and hold it, which would not be the case with the general public.

Does the hon. minister suppose that that stock shall be held perpetually in the hands of the Grand Trunk Company without dividends ? What is the object of having the stock If it is mere waste paper ? It is only valuable for its dividend-earning powers. You might just as well have so much waste paper unless it is going to earn a dividend. What possible advantage would there be in, the Grand Trunk Railway Company taking this $25,000,000 of stock unless it were going to have some dividend-earning power ? It is immaterial whether it is in the strong-box of the Grand Trunk Company or in the hands of the individuals ; it is bound to be taken into consideration by a commission considering the question of freight rates. They would take into consideration the amount of bonds on the road, the amount of interest, the amount of the common stock, and on all that they would base their decision on the question whether the rates were undue or not. In what other way could they arrive at a decision ? The company would claim that the whole amount of the stock should be considered, particularly as the Grand Trunk Railway Company might say :	We gave par value for
this stock ; we gave it, of course, in the way of privileges and rights and powers ; but it was par value. There is no way of preventing that, even if those rights and privileges were not worth five cents on the dollar. Who is to tell what their value is except the Grand Trunk Railway Company themselves ? And, as has been pointed out, that company is really the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. Who is to establish the value but the Grand Trunk Railway itself, which Is really the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ?

On the question of freight rates, the difference between this and previous contracts for building railways in that western country is very wide and important. The difference is so important that the people in that western country, who are interested, must see it at a glance. In the Canadian Pacific Railway contract there is a condition that there can be no interference with freight rates until 10 per cent is earned on the capital stock. In this contract there is no such provision. The whole question of I freight rates, east and west, will be under

the direction of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council or the railway commission to be constituted. That is the vital distinction. In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, no matter what the conditions may be, this parliament cannot interfere, until such a time as 10 per cent is earned on the capital stock, with the freight rates at all, without committing a great breach of faith. But in the case of this company, there is no such provision. The only condition regulating freight rates is the general law regarding railway companies, and that is of such a vital, important difference that it must impress itself at once on the public mind.
That does not cover the question that my hon. friend from King's has brought up concerning the bond issue.

I was just coming to that. If this stock were in the position of the ordinary stock of a railway company, if it could be placed on the market say at ten cents on the dollar, or put into the hands of first promoters at that rate, and that ten cents was alii that entered the treasury, and if, after the lapse of years, it went into the hands of innocent third parties, who paid a hundred cents on the dollar for it, these parties could come forward, when the question of adjusting the rates was brought up, and say with much force : We are entitled to a fair return on our investment of 100 cents on the dollar. There would be much force In that plea ; because, although ten cents only went into the treasury originally, the subsequent purchasers paid 100 cents, and would claim to be entitled to a dividend on the amount they paid. But we are protecting the people against any such condition, because we are refusing the company the power to put a dollar's worth of that stock on the market and sell it to any one. It is not negotiable, it cannot go on the stock market, it cannot be the subject of speculation ; no innocent third party will be able to come and say : I paid in good faith 100 cents in the dollar for that stock and am entitled to get a dividend on what I paid. We have stipulated that the stock cannot be put on the market, but must remain in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway during the term of this lease.
Is the road not supposed to earn a dividend on that stock while it is in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway ?

Probably it will. We hope it will. I am glad to see that my hon. friend is taking a more hopeful view of it. We have so much faith in the enterprise that we believe that It will earn a good deal of money, and I am glad my hon. friend takes that view.
And would that stock not be entitled to be taken into account just as if it were held by a third person ?

Exactly; but there is this difference, that if it were sold to third parties, these parties could justly claim that the price they paid should be considered when the freight rates were being regulated, and that the freight rates should be regulated so as to give them a return on what they paid, and not merely give a return on what the original holders of the stock paid for it. But in this case the stock must remain in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway ; and when it becomes necessary to regulate freight rates, the railway commission will take into account, not the nominal value of the stock, but the amount which the Grand Trunk Railway put into the road in return for that stock. The stock will remain in the treasury during the term of this lease at whatever value the Grand Trunk Railway put into it. and the Grand Trunk Railway will be obliged to show the railway commission exactly what value they gave, and that only will be taken into consideration in adjusting the freight rates.
That would be an excellent reason for adopting the amendment. I think that the difficulty is that there is no way of fixing the value given by the company.
The railway commission can fix it.
When the stock is wvn-tk 10 cents, or 15 cents, or 20 cents in the dollar ?
Whenever it is necessary.
If you would adopt this amendment you would fix it at once. I see that the Prime Minister laughs at that, but we would fix it at once at 100 cents in the dollar.
And suppose the Grand Trunk,1 Railway only put in value to the extent of 50 cents on the dollar, what then ?

The difficulty is this, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway may put a fictitious value upon the stock they give the Grand Trunk Railway, and I have here a provision to ensure that 100 cents on the dollar will be given for it.

If the hon. gentleman's object is to have no fictitious value, he should oppose this amendment. By the amendment you are giving that stock a value of 100 cents on the dollar, but nobody supposes that when it is issued it will be worth anything near that. No doubt its value will increase in time, but when issued its only value will be the confidence which the enterprise inspires in the market. If we were to allow the stock to be put on the public market, the value would be fixed by what the public would

be willing to pay for it, and that would be determined by the confidence which _ the investing public might have in the project. But we are providing that the stock must remain in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway, and we are doing this in order to protect the public. So long as this lease lasts, this capital stock must remain in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway ; and in any adjustments of freight l'ates, they will only be entitled to .such rates as will pay a dividend on the actual money put into the enterprise in exchange for the stock. By the amendment my hon. friefid wants that matter to be determined at once at 100 cents on the dollar, but it might be much less. My hon. friend from Hamilton, who has presented his views with that logic which always characterizes bis utterances, says that the two companies are one, and that the stock is to be taken by the Grand Trunk Railway ; and he asked, How is the value to be determined between them ? Well, the value is to be determined by the needs of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will require money to carry on its enterprise. If it needs the whole $25,000,000, the amount of this capital stock at par, it will have to get it, and it can only get it front the Grand Trunk Railway. In such a case, the value of the stock will be its par value, because that will be the amount which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway requires in return for its stock and which the Grand Trunk Railway will have to pay. The value of the stock will be fixed by the needs of the company, and cannot be fixed in any other way.
Has the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway not also the right to issue preference stock and bonds ?

Yes, but the Grand Trunk Railway has to guarantee this issue of stock and bond and carry on this enterprise, the cost of which has been estimated by hon. gentlemen opposite much higher than I think it will be. Between the bonds and the stock, I dlo not think the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have inordinate power. But suppose they have, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will have to issue that stock to the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Company has no interest in paying more for that stock than they must. If they can get it at 5 cents on the dollar they will try to do so. Suppose that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway only want $5,000,000, the value of that stock would be 20 cents on the dollar. And if the Grand Trunk advanced $5,000,000, as pointed out by the Minister of Finance, that will be the whole charge on the public with respect to that part of the common stock. Before the commission, in the fixing of rates, it will be shown that the Grand Trunk Company paid only $5,000,000, and it will be insisted that they should not draw Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
dividends on more than that sum. What is the policy of my hon. friend (Mr, Barker) ? He wants the enterprise to be loaded at once with $25,000,000, and the amount to go into the treasury of the Grand Trunk Pacific, so that, for all time, the settlers in the North-west will have to pay rates which will yield interest on this $25,000,000. It is hardly to be wondiered at that hon. gentlemen on this side who are interested in the people of the North-west object to such a proposal.

I am surprised at the argument of the hon. Prime Minister. He assumes to say that my desire is that this $25,000,000 shall be made a charge upon the enterprise, whether necessary or not. What could be more absured than a statement of that kind ? If the Grand Trunk Pacific get from the Grand Trunk $25,000,000 for, this common stock, it would not be necessary for them to issue so large an amount of bonds as if they received less for their stock. What is proposed here would not impose a greater burden, but a much less burden upon the people who have to pay freight rates on this road.
The hon. gentleman assumes that the stock is worth 100 cents on the dollar when it is issued, yet he knows that that is absurd.

It can be made worth that. If the law provides that it shall be issued at par, it must be issued at par. And, if you wish to prevent collusion between the two joints of this double-jointed company, the way to do it is to adopt the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton. As to the cost of construction, sections 28 and 34 clearly show that terminal facilities and all these things are covered by the term ' cost of construction.' That would include the branch lines as well as the western division, because, as has been pointed out, they are not obliged to build one of these branch lines, if they did, it is covered by the words ' cost of construction.' And it is provided for, as the bonds are guaranteed by the government to the extent of seventy-five per cent and the rest by the company, and that is covered by the mortgage. Then you have $20,000,000 of preference stock to cover the cost of equipment. I do not understand' why the government should object to accepting this amendment, unless from pride. They may think they have a perfect contract, and may have made up their minds that it shall not be amended. It seems to me that parliament ought to try to make this as perfect a Bill as possible. Such pride on the part of the government would not be proper pride. On other occasions they have benefited by suggestions of the members of the opposition, and have not been above accepting those suggestions. Therefore, I would urge upon the right hon. Prime Minister that he would accept the reasonable and very proper am-

eudment of the hon. member for Hamilton.

It seems to me that if we had a very pronounced difference of opinion before between the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister, we have that difference emphasized now. I understood the Minister of Justice to argue that this $25,000,000 was to be paid for in cash or the equivalent of cash. But, the Prime Minister says that would be a most deplorable condition of affairs for it would load the company with a debt of $25,000,000, but that, if the Grand Trunk should acquire this stock at 20 cents on the dollar it would load the enterprise with a debt of only $5,000,000.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) remember drawing my attention to the words ' due regard being had to the then market value of the stock.'
I do. I brought that to the hon. gentleman's attention, and may do so again before I get through. Are we to take the view of the Prime Minister or the view of the Minister of Justice ?
There is no difference.

When the hon. Prime Minister says there is no difference, that is the most remarkable statement that has been made this afternoon. The Minister of Justice has been convincing us-or rather, endeavouring to convince us, for I cannot say he has succeeded very well- that, from the very nature of things, the whole of this $25,000,000 must be paid by the Grand Trunk Railway Company in cash, or the equivalent in cash.
No, no.
If that is not the hon. gentleman's statement, I do not understand the English language.

Within the last half hour the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) stated directly that it was to be paid for in cash or the equivalent of cash, so far as was covered by the market value-not beyond that.

The Minister of Justice called attention to the fact that it was necessary for this company to construct terminal facilities and branch lines, and said, as distinctly as the English language would enable him to say it, that this fact made it necessary for this company to pay, either in cash or the equivalent of cash, the whole $25,000,000. He said that or he said nothing, and the hon. gentleman never rises in this House without saying something. I pointed out, at the time, that this was diametrically opposed to what the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid I.aur-ler) had stated when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company's charter was going
through the House. And the right hon. gentleman did not rise to make any correction. And now he has risen to say exactly what he said before, and to confuse two things which are absolutely and diametrically different ; namely, the market value of stack after it has been issued and the subscription rate of stock before it is put on the market at all. Surely, my hon. friend, on a moment's considerate n, will understand. For instance, the right hon. gentleman may to-morrow subscribe for stock on which he will pay 100 cents on the dollar, but. if he xiuts it on the market afterwards, it may not realize, at open sale, more than ten cents on the dollar. The two things are absolutely distinct and separate. The man who subscribes for stock in any joint stock corporation, in the absence of legislation to the contrary, must pay one hundred cents on the dollar for that stock, and the next day, if he attemps to sell the stock in the market, it may not be worth ten cents on the dollar. He subscribes and pays one hundred cents on the dollar because he has faith in the ultimate success of that enterprise, and he puts his money at risk by so subscribing. My hon. friend says it is a question of the Grand Trunk Company buying this stock. It is not a question of the Grand Trunk Company buying this stock, it is a question of the Grand Trunk Company subscribing for this stock, no one else is entitled to subscribe for it. In the absence of legislation to the contrary, the Grand Trunk Company must pay one hundred cents on the dollar for that stock. There is legislation to the contrary contained in clause 11 of the company's charter, and it is to meet the difficulty arising in connection with that, that my hon. friend from Hamilton has put this motion before the Committee. What possible reason is there for the Grand Trunk Railway Company, being to all intents and purposes the same thing, as the Minister of Finance has admitted, as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company-what possible reason is there that the Grand Trunk Company should have the right to subscribe for what is practically its own stock at twenty-five cents or ten cents on the dollar ? My right hon friend seems to think it is all right ; he seems to think it would be a calamity if the Grand Trunk Company should be obliged to pay $25,000,000 in value for $25,000,000 in stock. The Minister of Justice has referred to the words ' market value of the stock,' which are contained in clause 11 of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company's charter. It is for the very reason that these words are contained in that clause that my hon. friend from Hamilton has made his motion. Surely my right hon. friend has comprehended the argument to that extent. Here you have in clause 11 a provision by which the Grand Trunk Company can get this stock, not for cash but for something else than cash, and the value of that something else is to be

determined, not between two independent parties, but by two corporations which are to all intents and purposes, it is admitted, one corporation. There is no independent contract here, my bon. friend the Minister of Finance has stated that, my right hon. friend himself has stated that, there is no independent bargaining, which might be some safeguard to the public in ordinary cases. There is, as the Minister of Finance has said, using the apt expression which he appropriated-there is the same red-headed boy
That was not my expression.
My hon. friend adopted it with the utmost approval.
But I do not want to be credited with its origin.

He did not originate it, but he thought it was so good that he adopted it and used it, and I am following his example now. Here is the same red-headed boy on the one hand and on the other. This red-headed boy with one hand is fixing the value of the stock,, and with the other hand he is accepting the value of the stock so fixed. It is for that very reason that my hon. friend has brought this amendment to the attention of the House. Surely my right hon. friend will not persevere in his suggestion that it would be a calamity for this country and to these two corporations that the Grand Trunk Company should pay par value for the $25,000,000 of stock it is to receive. It imposes a burden upon the company ? I do not follow the right hon. gentleman in that suggestion at all. If the Grand Trunk Company pays par value for this stock and puts $25,000,000 into the enterprise, presumably it will be used wisely and prudently for the purposes of the company; and the people of this country, when they have to pay dividends on that in freight rates afterwards, will know that that money has gone into the purposes of the railway and that they have received some advantages in railway facilities, in terminal facilities, in something for the money upon which they are required to pay dividends. I suggest again to my hon. friend that when he takes the ground that it is a question of sale and not a question of subscription, he is not adhering to the usual condition of things, or to the terms of this contract itself. This stock is never to become the property of any other person, for a term of fifty years at least, than the Grand Trunk Company itself. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance savs that it can never be parted with by the Grand Trunk Company, and he bases an argument upon that. He is not correct in that, because after
I said during the fifty years.

Well, my hon. friend intended that, I do not think he made Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
it quite so plain as he thought, in the hurry of speaking. For a period of fifty years it is to be held by the Grand Trunk Company, but after that it can go into the hands of the public. This after all is not a question of sale in the market, it is a question of subscription by the Grand Trunk Company for this stock, but with this qualification which the right hon. gentleman uses for a purpose that is absolutely opposed to the real bearing. He says because you have the words ' market value ' here, that makes it a sale. That does not make it a sale, but it fixes the standard by means of which the Grand Trunk may subscribe for that stock. The Grand Trunk can pay less than the par value. That is the true significance of these words in section 11 of the clause, and that is the significance that we complain of, and it is for that reason that my hon. friend from Hamilton in submitting to the committee an amendment by which the Grand Trunk Company shall be obliged, if it acquires $25,000,000 of capital stock in this company, to pay $25,000,000 in cash for that stock so subscribed, in order that that sum of money may go into this enterprise for the purpose of affording to the people of this country the railway facilities which they are entitled to demand under an enterprise of so great moment as that which we are considering.

I think that my leader, while doing full justice to the care which has been shown in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway, has failed to do perfect justice to the astuteness with which the gentlemen who drew up the Bill have provided that the Grand Trunk Pacific must of necessity be squeezed by the Grand Trunk. We have heard a great deal about the market value of the stock, and no person can have listened to the discussion without feeling that the government side regard as one of the great safeguards which is relied upon, this felicitous expression, ' the market value of the stock.' I assume that the hon. gentlemen are sincere, and so for a moment I will asa. you to consider what precautions they have taken to secure that there shall not be any market value to the stock. If there was any amount of that stock that could be put on the market, then of course there Is a way of ascertaining the market value. But if you carefully provide that only $25,000,000 of stock is to be issued, and that the whole is to be taken up by one corporation, can anybody with the wildest imagination even suggest how the market value could be ascertained for such stock as that ? Now. the Premier, speaking of stocks generally, said with perfect accuracy that the value of stock is fixed by the public. We quite understand that. If stock is put on the market as all ordinary stocks are, its value depends on the confidence the public has in the enterprise, and the public displays its confidence by buying and selling that stock in the market. But how can you

take the money value of stock that you forbid to be put on the market, that you compel one company to hand over to another company by the very terms of the enactment ? It is an abuse of language, it seems like an attempt to throw dust in the eyes of the public, whin you compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to hand over the stock to the Grand Trunk, every dollar of it, and not only to be handrj over, but actually to be held by them fci the term of fifty years. I think the Premier will hardly say that it is possible that any market value could be fixed on stock handled in that way. But the right hon. gentleman was good enough to explain how he thought the value of the stock would be fixed. He said the value of this stock would he fixed by the need of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I entirely agree with him in that. Let us see what it means. The value of this stock, $25,000,000 worth, is to be fixed by the needs of the Grand Trunk Pacific ; therefore the less the Grand Trunk Pacific could get for that stock the greater will be its need ; the more they get the better off they will be. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have a certain amount of stock and that is of any value to them, it is to the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Compauv that the need of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall be as great as possible because the greater the need of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the less will be the value of the stock, so that the moment the needs of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are increased down goes the value of the stock.
Therefore, the more they will have to pay.

No, I am going to show that the line taken by the hon. member for King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler) is the accurate line there. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company need a certain amount of money, they have either to borrow it or to sell the stock, and if they sell the stock for $25,000,000, then they would only have to borrow $25,000,000 less than if they gave the stock to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for nothing. They only require so much money, and they can only get it from one of two sources-capital or borrowed money. The more they raise from their capital the less they will have to borrow, and the less they raise from their capital the more they will have to borrow. If the stock is handed over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for nothing or for a nominal figure, the more they will have to borrow. What will be the position then ? The hon. Minister of Finance says that the railway commissioners will take into consideration the value of this stock in fixing freight rates. I wonder if the hon. Minister of Finance really wishes the country to understand that with all the ability, skill and experience he possesses the best he can
suggest in the interest of the tax-payer and in the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is that, should they give the stock away, the commissioners will by and by keep down the rates so that the company will not be able to make any more than would pay dividends on the market value of the stock ? Surely, it would be expected, in the interest of the people who have to pay the taxes, that the hon. minister should see that this $25,000,000 is paid for at a hundred cents on the dollar, and that less money should be borrowed than if they had only obtained five or ten cents per share. Yet, he trusts to luck, despite all the ability and ingenuity that railway companies can exercise to get as much as possible out of the country, that the commissioners will be able to draw the line so finely between what the stock should be assessed at and what it has really been sold for that they can control rates in such a way as to ensure the condition that the people will not have to pay any more than is necessary to pay fair dividends on the stock. If this stock was handed over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company in consideration of giving a guarantee of $20,000,000 or $30,000,000, or whatever it may be, of the bonds, how are the commissioners to determine what the value of the stock was ? The two corporations would agree that the services rendered by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company were worth $25,000,000, and so this stock would be offered in full settlement of those services. How could the commissioners simply allow rates to be charged sufficient to pay dividends on what had been paid for this stock when both corporations agreed that the services rendered were worth $25,000,000 ?

I am afraid that at the risk of being unable to satisfy the hon. gentleman I will be obliged to repeat my argument and go a point further. Reference has been made to the public interest, but I must frankly confess that I failed to see where there is any public interest involved in this matter, save and except as touching freight rates of which I have spoken. This is a matter between the two joints of one company, if I may be allowed to put it in that way. I maintain that we are not at all concerned as to what these two companies do in reference to that. If it were stock that was to be placed on the market and sold, I could at once recognize that we would have a great deal of interest in it. If this stock were to be put upon the market and taken over by the Grand Trunk Railway Company-I will take the figures of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition for illustration-at 25 cents on the dollar, and in later years it passed into the hands of other people at 100 cents on the dollar, if the question of freight

rates comes to be adjusted at any time, and it becomes a question whether we are to have such freight rates as will earn a fair dividend on the 100 cents that the present holder paid or on the 25 cents that originally went into the treasury there certainly is much to be said in favour of the man who purchased the stock and who says : * I paid 100 cents on the dollar for it. 1 cannot help what was done five or ten years ago. I paid dollar for dollar for this stock, and I expect that the freight rates shall be adjusted accordingly.' But, we have prevented that in this case. Some of the Canadian Pacific Railway stock was put on the market at 25 cents on the dollar. To-day it is worth 100 and more. I do not know what the market quotation is to-day. If we were not subject to that 10 per cent clause, if that clause were repealed, and if we were dealing with the general operation of the Railway Act on a question of freight rates, there would be much free in the argument of the man who comes forward and says : ' I cannot help how much the stock went for originally. I paid $120 for the stock, and I am entitled to such rates as will give me a fair dividend om $120.' In that he would present a fairly debatable case. But, that condition cannot arise in this case. Now, let us take these two companies, or to use the illustration which has been used, the two sides of the same redheaded boy and I think that the strength of this enterprise is to be found in the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are not only behind it, but that they are in it and of it. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company take over this new stock at 25 cents on the dollar, they cannot sell it to anybody at 26 cents on the dollar the next day, and they cannot sell it later on for 100 cents on the dollar. It must stay in the treasury of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and if a question arises as to freight rates, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would be called upotn to show, mot what is the nominal value upon to show not what is the nominal value of the stock, not what somebody else has paid for the stock, but how much money or the equivalent of money was given by the Grand Trunk Railway Company originally for the stock. How then will the public have any earthly interest in the matter ? When that question arises it will not be trusting to luck. It will be trusting to the recognized tribunal established for the purpose of controlling railway rates, and when there is a case for consideration it will be for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to show that they paid a fair value either in money or the equivalent of money for the stock at that time, when it passed into their hands.

Surely the lion. Minister of Finance must see how utterly impossible it would be for the railway commissioners Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
five or ten years hence to form any judgment whatever as to the actual value given for the stock ? Here are two companies identically the same sitting down together as we have so often pointed out, and agreeing upon the value of certain rights and privileges and powers between one company and the other. Here we have these two companies agreeing according to this 11th section, upon the actual market value, an absolutely unknown quantity, of the stock, and saying that the stock and these privileges are equivalent to each other. Is it possible for any man in the world to point out any error in the contract made between the two parties ? The hon. gentleman knows it would be absolutely impossible, but whoever drew this contract has taken very good care that even that small protection shall be done away with. Let us see what the clause says :
The directors of the company elected by the shareholders may make and issue as paid up stock.
What does that mean ? The hon. gentleman knows that there will be $100,000 of this stock issued for the purpose of directors qualification, and beyond question 100 cents on the dollar will be paid in cash for that. Does the hon. gentleman suppose that the company can pay a different dividend on one part of this stock from what they pay on the other, when the statute under which they are created says the whole of it is paid-up stock '! Not only is it paid-up stock, but
The said issue and allotment of stock shall be binding ion thie company.
You provide here that the company shall not be permitted to depart from dealing with their stock as paid-up stock. You will have $100,000 of this stock paid in cash, and the balance of $24,900,000 is paid for by a dicker between the two companies; a dicker that no one can estimate hereafter. And yet, you say that the railway commission can determine that when they are fixing rates. The hon. gentleman must have started on that argument without reading the section.
I understood the Minister of Justice to say that the terminal facilities were not covered by these bonds.
I drew the attention of the leader of the opposition to section 18 of the charter, and I said it was the section that had reference to the bonds with respect to terminals.

I understood the Minister of Justice to challenge the member for Hastings to point out where there was any provision in the charter that bonds might be issued to eover the terminal facilities, and I also understood him to say that the $25,000.000 of common stock had to be taken in connection with the preference stock for the purpose of paying for these terminal facilities.

Not in connection with the preference stock; but it had to be taken into consideration in 'connection with the terminals, as in connection also with the construction of telegraph and telephone lines and other things of that character. My contention is, that the bond issue will not be sufficient for the construction of the main line, or the terminals, or the branch lines, and far from offering any challenge, I merely drew the attention of the leader of the opposition to section 18, as mv hon. tnend will see if he looks at ' Hansard.
I understood the minister to draw a distinction between the railway and the terminals.
Yes.
And to say that the terminals are not a part of the railway.
Of course they are a part of the railroad.
Then I cannot understand what the Minister of Justice means.

There is a bond issue and a certain portion of it will be guaranteed by the government and a certain portion by the Grand Trunk Company. I contend that the boind issue will not be sufficient for the construction of the terminals, or of the branch lines or of the main line, but that it will be necessary in addition to the bond issue to have the proceeds of this common stock to build the terminals.
Do I understand the minister to say that these bonds will not realize enough to build the road.
It is ray opinion that the second issue guaranteed by the Grand Trunk will not realize par.
What does the hon. minister think they will realize ?

I would not care to figure that out.
Mr. CLANCY'. I understood the Minister of Finance to say that the public were ini no sense concerned, except in so far as this contract affected freight rates.
I did not see where the public interest was concerned in this particular matter, except as to freight rates.

The supporters of the government laid great stress on the fact that the Grand Trunk in taking this $25,000,000 of common stock, added to the security that the country held for the carrying out of this work. If that be true, then the country is concerned both as to freight rates and as to the security we hold. But if the Prime Minister is right, that the Grand Trunk may acquire this stock for five cents on the
dollar, that security absolutely vanishes. If there was no guarantee of bonds I could understand that the public could not be concerned, but when we are taking this $25,000,000 of common stock as security, for which the Grand Trunk may pay only five cents on the dollar, then the country is deeply concerned. We are told that the Grand Trunk Railway Company was to take $25,000,000 of this stock and that that was to-be a security
If my hon. friend means that I said, or that an'v one else said, that the Grand Trunk would put up $25,000,000 in cash in return for this common stock, he is mistaken. I said nothing of the kind.
Where is the security that the Grand Trunk Railway gives if they do not put up the money, when" we are guaranteeing the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific?

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is wrong. We are not guaranteeing them in the sense in which he uses the word. We are only guaranteeing a portion and they must from their various resources, of which this is one, obtain the balance to carry out this great undertaking.
I have never said that the $25,000,000 of common stock is in itself, apart from other things, a very great security. But it is worth something in connection with the other tilings which the Grand Trunk has to give as guarantee. The Grand Trunk and its associates, as promoters, have to provide a large sum for rolling stock, and other things. I did not for a moment stop to consider how much in actual cash or equivalent to cash this common stock will bring, but in any observations that I have made, I have never looked upon it as being in itself a security to the value of $25,000000 in cash.

I want to say one word with reference to what the hon. Finance Minister has said. I followed his first speech endeavouring to ascertain what position the Grand Trunk Company would occupy towards the public with reference to the $25,000,000 of stock. The hon gentleman said that if the Grand Trunk Company did not pay the full value for that stock, in the adjustment of rates afterwards, they would not be permitted to rank as creditors who had paid full value for it. I recognize the justness of that ; but the Finance Minister did not fully state this matter.
I undertake to say that the old Grand Trunk Company can get that $25,000,000 of stock, and rank as! having full value for it under the terms of this contract. If it is desirable to prevent them, language must be introduced into this contract different from what exists in it now. I understood from the Finance Minister that it was desirable that they should not be allowed to rank as creditors who had paid one hundred cents on the



dollar for the $25,000,000 of stock, unless they actually had contributed that amount to the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the old Grand Trunk are two railway coi-porations, clear and distinct in their transactions. They have the best of counsel, and when they sit down to do business, they will do it in a thorough manner that will hold water against a railway commission or anybody else. The hon. member for Hamilton has stated this matter in a way that commands my utter acquies-1 cenoe as a business man and a lawyer-that if you want the Grand Trunk Company to get no undue advantage from this $25,000,000 of stock, you must make them pay full value for it. In the 11th section of the Grand Trunk Pacific charter, there is very-ingenious language, which I have no doubt was put there by railroad lawyers, who understood this thing a great deal better than the Finance Minister or myself or perhaps anybody else in this House ; possibly better than the Minister of Justice, who has perhaps not had a wide experience in railway promotion and railway law. I undertake to say that there are railway lawyers in this country who can frame clauses which will deceive us all, of which we will never know the full import until we get before a court. In the last resort the court must construe these clauses as the language forces them. I will undertake to say that when this stock passes, the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific can enter into an agreement that will prevent any railway commission disturbing their arrangement. Under clause 11, of the Grand Trunk Pacific charter, the company is permitted to issue common stock in return for services rendered. That is very broad language; I will only deal with these two words. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company are permitted to hand around their common stock for everything but promotion services, and especially, in the express language of the Act, they can give it for services rendered. If the Grand Trunk Pacific are going to hand over $25,000,000 of their common stock to the old Grand Trunk, what will they do ? They will have that agreement put in the form of a deed, by competent lawyers. In that deed it will be recited that the Grand Trunk have rendered services to the Grand Trunk Pacific, by helping them to sell their bonds or their stock, or perhaps by carrying freight ; and the Grand Trunk Pacific can say, for these services we agree to pay the old Grand Trunk Company $25,000,000, and wc hereby hand over, in discharge of that indebtedness, $25,000,000 of stock. Suppose that agreement takes the form of a deed, both sides are estopped from disputing it thereafter, and no court can upset it. Consequently the hon. Minister of Finance did not make his point clear and sound. The whole question is open, and the Grand Trunk Pacific could to-morrow hand over to the
old Grand Trunk Company $25,000,000 of stock for services rendered, and no railway commission could afterwards inquire into the transaction. That could be charged as an outlay, which the Grand Trunk Pacific would be entitled to have regarded as money put into the road, and no court would dispute their contention. If the hon. Minister of Finance thinks the value of the stock should be taken into account by the railway commission, in fixing freight rates, lie has this fact staring him in the face, that the $25,000,000 of stock given to the Grand Trunk Company will form a basis for the establishment of those rates. The hon. gentleman has referred to the provision in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract that the rates on that railway cannot be regulated until the company earn 10 per cent on the money invested in it. That was a very wise provision at the time, and was necessary to induce capitalists to invest in the undertaking. We are in an altogether different position to-day, and this contract may work out much more disadvantageously, because if the whole $25,000,000 of stock is made to rank against the Grand Trunk Pacific, we may find that the rates may have to be fixed to give that company far more than 10 per cent. There is this advantage in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract, that when the company earns 10 per cent we can interfere, no matter wliat case they may make out before the railway commission ; but in this case we could not interfere, even if the company made more than 10 per cent, so long as this stock could be established ns chargeable against the company. It would be a gross outrage to refuse to give a railway company an opportunity to earn a fair interest rate on the money put into it. We must look ahead to see that the railway commission are not required to face a difficulty of this kind. I undertake to say, notwithstanding everything that lias been put forward by the Minister of Finance, that if this clause is left in the Rill, the railway commission will he forced to face the claim that $25,000,000 has been paid in by the old Grand Trunk Railway Company. Will there be no doubt or difficulty on that score ? It seems to me that the provision of my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that the Grand Trunk should pay $25,000,000 is the only guarantee the Canadian people can have. Then there will be no question as the money will have gone into the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. And in such case we will not have the bonds and other charges to meet, but will have a fair deal. The $25,000,000 will be paid in and the public will get the benefit. Rut if you leave this clause as it is. you leave it to the two companies to settle between themselves the amount for which the Grand Trunk Company should rank against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. No court will go behind the deed of agreement be-
tweeu the two parties. The court will hold that by this clause it is contemplated that that agreement should be binding upon all parties.

I do not like to disturb the very interesting and able argument put forward by the hon. gentleman, but perhaps he will bear in mind that it was the Railway Committee of which the hon. gentleman was a member, that was imposed upon when this section was drawn.
Very likely.
Who is to settle the value of the services ?

The only case in which value of the services will have to be determined will be in relation to the freight rates, and the railway commission will have authority to inquire into everything bearing on the freight rates, and any railway commission which would undertake to interpret the contract in the way my hon. friend interprets it ought to be dismissed without ceremouy.

The railway commission would have to be governed by the same judicial principles and rules of interpretation as the Supreme Court of Canada. Suppose the railway commission were confronted by an agreement between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, containing a recital of the services done and fixing the value of those services at $25,000,000, could it go outside of that ? I am not very captious.
No, just a little.

I followed the Prime Minister very attentively and I must say he gave me a great deal more light on the subject than did the Minister of Justice. I think the right hon. gentleman had better take charge of the legal part of the contract The Prime Minister takes the view that this stock will be paid for by the Grand Trunk Railway-and that it is only what the Grand Trunk Railway pays which will be charged against the company. But how do you propose to determine what value has been given by the Grand Trunk Railway ?
How are you going to control these two companies when they make a deed of sale from one to the other of that stock ? Suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway 3521
And I might add that it is inconceivable that the hon. gentleman should have allowed himself to be so imposed upon.
I ought to apologize then to the hon. minister
1 do not want an apology but simply wish to state the facts.

Perhaps the committee were much more innocent that the Minister of Justice would have been. If he had been on the committee, no doubt these loose words would never have got in and the Minister of Finance would never have been called on to make so inconsequential an argument. He makes better arguments as a rule. I am glad, for the sake of the Minister of Justice, that he made that explanation.
This was never before the Railway Committee.
What ? We are talking about section 11 of the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend does not know what Bill we are discussing.

What words could be looser', put in an Act of parliament, than these words, ' services rendered' ? I have confined myself, entirely, to the argument with reference to these words; and have not spoken of the words, in the first part of the section, almost equally extraordinary. For instance, you have the expression,
' paid-up stock.' There is a great deal of difficulty, in the country, owing to Acts of parliament, which say that certain stock shall be considered fully paid up. There has been great litigation, in our part of the country, over such expressions. People in Nova Scotia, who have got charters, hold that

they are entitled to give stock as remuneration for services, to promoters and others. Then, creditors of the company have used these people, in the courts, to make them pay up their shares, notwithstanding the words, which apparently provide, that these shares should be considered paid up. A great deal of litigation has been engendered.
1 believe that the current of the decisions has been against those who seek to hold their shares without paying for them in cash. These words with regard to issuing a paid-up stock are dangerous, if you count upon such stock not ranking before the railway commission the same as stock paid for in cash. I think the railway commission would say :	Parliament, sitting as parliament, and making laws, declared that this stock should be considered as paid up, if paid for by services rendered, no measure being given for those services. Suppose that the company asked me.for a legal opinion, and, on giving it. I made a demand for a million dollars, aind they gave me stock for that amount, I would like to know how the Minister of Finance would keep me from ranking, before the railway commission, just the same as though I had paid for that stock in cash. The company are permitted to issue that stock for services rendered, and they are the judges of the value of the services. Suppose the Minister of Finance rendered this company service-and his services would be valuable- and they handed him over $5,000,000 of stock, I would like to know what argument could be made before the railway commission to prevent him ranking the same as any other stockholder ? We must not look at this thing like children; we must not merely talk about these things without following them up to their legitimate conclusion. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has hit the nail squarely on the head. He says that, if you are going to avoid difficulty, if you are going to make the Grand Trunk Railway Company pay the full value of these shares, the only way is to provide that they are to pay for them in cash.

As between the two companies concerned, any agreement such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) refers to might stand, just as between two farmers dealing with a matter in which they are concerned, an agreement might stand. But when third parties come in, as the public come in in this case, no railway commission would recognize such a bargain as a bona fide investment. I cannot believe that any railway commission would take that extraordinary view. Any bargain made between these companies surely does not biind any tribunal representing the public.
How does the hon. gentleman get over the wording of section 11 '!

The Minister of Justice has stated that section 11 was passed by the Railway CommitHpe. That is qujte true. But the hon. gentleman did not tell all. This clause was strenuously objected to in the committee by the opposition members. And, when, the matter came to this House, I had the honour to move an amendment to this section along the lines of the amendment now proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton. So, the horn. Minister of Justice was not quite fair in saying that this section passed the Railway Committee in its present form; for, not only in the Railway Committee, but on the third reading in this House, it was only passed by the force of the majority, against the most strenuous objection on the part of the opposition. We are not taking a different position now from that which we took when the Grand Trunk charter was before the House.

The Minister of Finance practically adopted the view which the Prime Minister adopted, as I understood him, namely, that this section No. 11 was inserted in order that the Grand Trunk Railway Company might obtain the $25,000,000 of common stock for less than par value, because, as he says, otherwise you could not expect any corporation to go into an enterprise of this kind. That is not quite consistent with the argument of the Minister of Justice. Nor is it consistent with the view expressed by another Minister of the Crown who spoke on another stage of this Bill. The view of this minister is that this enterprise is of so doubtful a character that you could not expect people to put money into it and pay par value for the stock.
People do mot do it in railways generally.

But the hon. gentleman has forgotten that a clause allowing that has been struck out of the Railway Act by the very government of which he is a member, a clause which did not go nearly so far as this one. That clause was struck out. on objection being raised on this side of the House, at the instance of the then Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) as a clause which should not appear in our general Railway Law. That view presented by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals speaking at that time on behalf of the government, is not at all in harmony with the view that the Minister of Finance presents to the House this afternoon. But, departing from that for a moment, does my hom. friend the Minister of Finance regard this enterprise of building a railway through the western part of Canada of so doubtful a character that it is necessary that $25,000,000 worth of stock should be handed over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for say 25 cents, or 10 cents, on the dollar ? I should hardly have expected my non. friend the Minister of Finance to take that

position. And, let me tell him that in taking that position he expresses a view diametrically opposed to that put forward by his colleague, the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton). If he will refer to the speech, the very important speech, delivered by the Minister of the Interior on the second reading of the Bill he will find expressions which would indicate that that lion, gentleman, speaking for the government, regarded this enterprise of building a railway through the west as absolutely bound to afford a splendid return on every dollar invested in it. Now the Minister of Finance, who follows in this regard the leader of the government, practically tells the House and country that that enterprise is of so doubtful a character that we must dispose of stock at 25 cents, or 10 cents, on the dollar, in order to get corporations or individuals interested in the enterprise. Let us see what the Minister of the Interior thought about it:
But this new line of the Grand Trunk Pacific will run from Winnipeg to the Mountains, pass through a belt every mile of which is fertile and productive. It is hardly conceivable that such should be the case, yet the information in the possession of the government amply justifies the statement that I have made.
That is the view of the Minister of the Interior, in direct contradiction to that which has been expressed by my right bon. friend and the Minister of Finance. But he went on further :
The Grand Trunk Pacific, on the other hand, will go

He is contrasting it with the Canadian Pacific Railway. He has pointed out that the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day is yielding a magnificent dividend on all the capital which was invested in that company, and he is showing by way of contrast, that the Grand Trunk Pacific is a very much better proposition that that of the Canadian Pacific Railway :
The Grand Trunk Pacific, on the other hand, will go from the Rocky Mountain pass to the coast through as rich a timber and agricultural country as there is in Canada-a country rich in timber, mineral and soil.
Then to emphasize his point he goes on further :
Then we must not forget that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was projected, there was no movement of settlement from the outside. There were no farmers coming to Canada in 1881 from foreign countries. Ait any rate their number was inappreciable, and the Canadian Pacific Railway suffered from that fact. That company had dozens of agents out trying to initiate movements of population into our western country but did not succeed to any considerable extent, and for years later there was practically no immigration of any serious volume into the North-west Territories or upon the lands from which the Canadian Pacific Railway had to draw its traffic. What movement of population there was came almost entirely from the eastern provinces. But what is the
position now ? We had an immigration into the Nor.th-we3t of 30,000 people last year. If it keeps on at that rate for the next ten years, think what that will mean for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Think of the difference in the position of that company as compared with that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which went travelling on for years and years before there was any appreciable influx of settlers. Let it be remembered also that when the Canadian Pacific Railway started business, it had no connections with eastern Canada and no way of getting business. What had it to do ? It had to go to Montreal and set to work at an enormous sacrifice to parallel the Grand Trunk Railway by connections all over Canada. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, on the contrary, w'ill start with a magnificent system of connections, ready to open business the very day the road is finished.
Now, in view of that statement on behalf of the government by the Minister of the Interior, what ground has the Prime Minister, or what ground has the Minister of Finance for suggesting as an argument to defeat the proposition of my hon. friend from Hamilton, that no corporation in this country could be induced to go into this enterprise unless they are to receive stock at very much less than its par value ? Why, in the description of this enterprise given by the Minister of the Interior in the speech to which I have referred, he says that that enterprise is calculated, so far as the western portion of it is concerned, to yield magnificent dividends, dividends of 8, 10 and 12 per cent upon every dollar put into It, and not only would yield that, but yield it from the very commencement of the enterprise. Yet the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance seem to think, for some reason which they have not made clear, which I cannot very well understand, that there should be $25,000,000 of common stock of this railway handed over to the Grand Trunk for ' some unknown compensation, which, obviously, in view" of section 11 of the charter, is to be very much less than the par value of the stock. What is the explanation of this on the part of the government ? Why, we have had, it seems to me, a remarkable spectacle here this afternoon. My right hon. friend takes one view, the Minister of Justice takes another view, and the Minister of Finance takes one which is not quite the same as either, hut very much resembles that of the Prime Minister. What is the view of the government in regard to this ? Does the government state that the whole of this money is to he paid up in cash or its equivalent, as the Minister of Justice argues : or does the government, as the Prime Minister has stated, believe it necessary for the success of this enterprise that $25,000,000 in stock should be handed over to the Grand. Trunk ? What is the position of the government with regard to that ? Surely my right hon. friend will give his reasons, the reasons which induced him to depart so absolutely from the view which was taken by the

Minister of the Interior in the speech to which I hare alluded.

I am glad to hear that my hon. friend, by reading this quotation from the Minister of Finance, finds something in the way of commendation of this great enterprise. After reading iso much about the muskegs and everything else disparaging to that country, it is a pleasure to discover, even though it comes in the way of a quotation

I object to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) interrupting me in this way ; as an old parliamentarian he knows better. I want to say that after all that we have heard in the way of discrediting this great enterprise, it is a delight to us to find that hon. gentlemen opposite are now beginning to see some merits in it. I believe it will in due time pay a fair return on the capital; but it is not inconsistent with that to say that many a great enterprise which is placed before the country and which proves a profitable and successful enterprise, does not value its stock at 100 cents on the dollar ; and even though this stock should be placed in the hands of the Grand Trunk Company at less than 100 cents, it does not follow that the enterprise will not be a great success.
Mi-. BORDEN (Halifax). I am not aware that any hon. gentleman has made any disparaging suggestions with regard to the western part of this railway. The hon. gentleman is not quite candid in making that statement. Further than that, my right hon. friend has not said one word in reply to my statement of the attitude of his own government in striking out from the General Railway Act the very words upon which he is relying now. Why did the government take that attitude from the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals only a few weeks ago, and why does it now take a precisely different attitude with regard to this company, in the exceptional circumstances which I have mentioned, where the bargain which is to be made with regard to this stock is not really between two independent parties at all, but is between two joints of the same company, as the Minister of Finance has explained a few moments ago ?
