My hon. friend the Minister of Finance in some high sounding phrases, tells us that it is of great importance that the Grand Trunk Company should he in and of this contract. It is not in and of this contract at all except that it can control this company without incurring any obligation on its part with regard to the stipulations of this contract. Make it truly and really, in some sense at least, and of this contract by providing that as long as it controls the policy of this company it shall see to it that the Grand Trunk Pacific does carry out in good faith the stipulations, conditions and covenants contained on behalf of that company in this contract. I therefore submit, Mr. Chairman with every confidence in its merits, the provisions of the this amendment for the consideration of the government, believeing that, taking the very serious statements of members on the treasury benches into consideration, the govern-raent will see that there is a real danger, and they will see that some measure of relief at least against that danger can be

afforded by bringing the Grand Trunk Railway Company really and trully in and of this contract, and make it liable in case the Grand Trunk Pacific should see fit not to observe the covenants and stipulations in this contract contained.

The answer to my hon. friend's argument is a very obvious one. My hon. friend has premised the whole of the amendment which he has just proposed to the committee upon an opinion expressed by my colleague the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) in a speech which he delivered upon the second reading of this Bill. My hon. friend, however, only stated part of the argument of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce ; in fact, the opinion to which my hon. friend called the attention of the committee and which had been expressed by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce was simply in support of the Bill which is now before the House. My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave numerous reasons in favour of this scheme being ratified by parliament, and then he stated this further reason:	The Grand Trunk Railway Company have already connections as far as Chicago. There is only a distance as the crows fly, of 700 miles between Chicago and Winnipeg. Pass this Bill and the Grand Trunk Railway Company will have no interest in building a line from Chicago to Winnipeg in order to have connection from Winnipeg by way of Chicago, because you have given them this connection by way of North Bay, Toronto and Montreal by this new line of railway. Reject this Bill and you force the Grand Trunk Railway Company to get connections by way of Chicago. That is the argument that he presented to the House, and therefore, my hon. friend failed altogether to appreciate the force of the argument that was presented by my right hon. friend on that occasion. The argument of my right hon. friend is a very obvious one. I forget if he made the argument as complete as I make it now, but he made it in a very obvious manner. The moment that this Bill, which we have now before us is passed, the Grand Trunk Railway Company have no interest in building a' line from Winnipeg to Chicago. That seems to me to be a very sound reason, and everybody will agree that my right hon. friend was right when be said that the moment this railway is built, the moment the Grand Trunk Railway Company have connection by the road which the government propose to build from North Bay to Winnipeg, the Grand Trunk Railway Company have no interest whatever in expending money for building a road to get access to the prairie country, because they have already access to the prairie country by a road which is now contemplated and which is submitted for the approval of parliament.
Then, the answer to my hon. friend is that the government did not think that there was any necessity for providing any more security against the Grand Trunk Railway Company building by way of Chicago, because the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, as stated in the argument of my right hon. friend, ceases completely, falls to the ground the moment this Bill is ratified and the railway is built. If we built the railway between Winnipeg and North Bay, using the railway which is now contemplated by the government of Ontario, and which would connect with this road near Lake Abitibi, what interest would the Grand Trunk Railway have in expending a large sum of money to provide a railway which would be a very expensive railway to construct between Chicago and Winnipeg ? The interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company Is to get traffic into their territory, and they will bring it more easily and at less cost by the project which is now before parliament than in any other way. Therefore, there is no necessity for providing against the contingency which my hon. friend has in mind. The same thing applies to the Portland division. When the road is built, as it will be built, from Winnipeg to Lake Abitibi, one has only to look at the map to see that there will be no fear of any competition from Portland, because, when a train has come to the longitude of Lake Abitibi, it will be far nearer Quebec than Portland. It will be less than 500 miles from Quebec and almost 700 miles from Portland. We think we have every precaution against the contingency which my hon. friend had in view, because the very merit of the scheme which we have now before us will be the best guarantee against American competition. I do not see the relevancy of the amendment which my hon. friend has just moved, to the idea which he has expressed in the speech which he has delivered. Do I understand my hon. friend to say that he is not quite sure of his own amendment, and that he proposes to supplement it later on ?

I have declared in this amendment the expediency of imposing upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company all the obligations, which, by the terms of this agreement, are imposed upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I have taken the safe-guards, whatever they were, which the government had included in the contract, and I have applied these safe-guards to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and what I said was that I did not think the provisions contained in the agreement in that regard were as adequate as they might be. and that while moving this amendment. I did not want to be understood as embodying in it everything which one might think might be done to I lessen the danger that was spoken of by

the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. For the present all I am doing is to take the language of the government itself in the agreement, and to say that these obligations imposed upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall also be obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
As respects the new road
As respects everything under the agreement.
The western section of the road as well as the eastern section 1
Yes.
The new construction altogether ?
Yes.
I understood that my hon. friend contemplated the possibility of adding to his amendment.

Yes, my right hon. friend is quite correct. I have only had 48 hours to deal with the matter, and I thought that possibly I might be able to suggest something later on which I myself would regard as a little more effective than that which I am proposing at the present time.

What I want to say is that as my hon. friend contemplates the possibility of improving his amendment we had better let section 7 stand in the meantime.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 8,

One of my hon. friends has some amendments to propose to this section. He was under the impression that the amendments that I moved would be more fully discussed, and he is therefore not quite prepared to proceed.

We will allow the section to stand.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 9,

Before you proceed with this section, I would suggest that we might advantageously substitute the words ' the operation thereof ' for its management,' so that it may read :
The construction of the said eastern division and the operation thereof until completed, &c.
The section as it stands was copied from the Bill to construct the Intercolonial Rail-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
way, and I am not quite sure that the words ' its management ' would suit in this case.

The suggestion made by the Minister of Justice opens up a subject of very great importance. I can quite understand that the necessity for the word ' operation ' presents itself to the mind of the minister, because for some years there will be large sections of this road completed which will have to be operated by the government. Has the government any suggestion to make as to how these sections will be operated before the time arrives when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be under obligation to take a lease of the road. The Grand Trunk Pacific are not under obligation to enter into the operation of the eastern section until the whole 1900 miles are completed. It is obvious that there may be sections, several hundred miles long, completed from time to time, and the House ought to be told what the idea of the government is as to operation in the interval, which may be five or six years. The government should be able to tell us this. It is all very well to say that it shall be operated by the commissioners, but it will have to be equipped. I do not suppose for a moment that the government contemplate leaving large sections of road constructed and not operated, because if so the embankments will wash away, the ties will rot, and the road will go to pieces. You cannot operate it without rolling stock, bias the government any idea of the loss that will be sustained in working sections of that kind ? What is the government going to do under these circumstances ?

All that is necessary at present is to make provision that if any section of this road is in a condition to be operated, it shall be at the option of the commissioners, who will act in conjunction with the government, to operate it themselves ; or to lease it to the Grand Trunk Company if they are ready to take it, or, by other arrangement that may be found convenient to operate the road temporarily until the time of completion. I do not know that at the present stage we are called upon to go beyond that. All these questions are important, and they will come up in due course. The theory of the whole scheme is that, we shall press forward the construction of this road with all possible speed, and all that is necessary now is to make provision that pending the completion and leasing of this road, the commissioners, or any responsible body with which they may make an arrangement, shall be empowered to operate the road.

Surely the government are not asking parliament to authorize the operation of 500 miles of railway, probably for five years, without telling us how they intend to equip that 500 miles with locomotives and rolling stock. It is going to cost a

considerable sum of money. Are we going to go it blind, and- are we to enter on this hastily and without any consideration, as the government appear to have done ? Are we to blindly vote a power of attorney to the government of the day to appoint a commission who will do just as it pleases. Here are 500 miles of railway completed through a new country, which the government think we consider to be muskegs and tilled with jackpines ; through this section of the country we w-ill have a road of 500 miles, which is not to be taken over by the lessees for several years, and which will lie idle unless parliament votes a very large sum of money for its equipment. Surely the government have considered this before submitting such a scheme to parliament. They must have intended to operate the road. They had the word ' management ' in, but the word ' oper-tion ' is much better. But even under the word ' management' they must have intended to operate it. They must have considered where they were going to get the cars and locomotives, and above all, where they were going to get the traffic. What is the government going to ? Have they any idea ?

~I do not think there is anything like going it blind in the matter. It will be precisely in the same position as any other road during the period of its construction. It will be the policy of the government to press forward the construction of this road with all speed that is consistent with efficient and economical construction, and if any portion of that road is in a condition to be operated before the time is reached at which we can lease it to the Grand Trunk Pacific, then unquestionably, if it is found in the public interest, as I have no doubt it will, that section will be operated. But parliament will meet once or twice before we have reached that stage, and I have no doubt there will be ample opportunity for dealing with these questions as they arise from time to time. There is no going it blind. We propose to build the road as quickly as possible, and. if any sections are available for operation before that moment comes to transfer it to the Grand Trunk Pacific, we must devise ways and means of operating it, either by the commissioners themselves, or, by leasing it to any other person or body corporate which can operate it.
The Minister of Finance fails to see the point I am raising. You cannot operate a road without rolling stock.
I did not say you could.
Has the government thought how they are going to do it ? Have they considered the question at nil ? Are they going to buy rolling stock for 500 miles of railway ?
Not this year.
But when it is completed ?
It is not going to be completed for a few months.

Then you have not thought it out at all. You are going to build it, and take chances when the road is completed. Does the minister seriously ask parliament to vote for the project under these circumstances ?
I do.

You do ? Then I am afraid that if the hon. gentleman were to go before a body of shareholders and tell them that is what he contemplates, they would ask him for some particulars. The hon. gentleman says it will be constructed as any other road would be by a company. But a road constructed by a company is put into operation as the sections are completed, because the company is going to continue to operate it. The hon. gentleman forgets for a moment that when this road is completed the government get out of its operation altogether, and they will have a lot of rolling stock on their hands which they will not know what to do with. The Grand Trunk Pacific will make a splendid bargain out of the government when they find them w7ith a large amount of rolling stock, and no place to put it. You will have to practically hand it over as a present to the Grand Trunk Pacific.

That will depend very much upon the wisdom of the government that is in power when this arrangement is made. We have a strong and abiding faith that there will be a wise go-ernment in power then.
Mr. BARKER, So have we.

We must depend upon the wisdom of the governments to guard the country against these foolish things which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) suggests. In the case of a company, if I were to go before a number of shareholders and tell them what I was going to do several years hence, in regard to these details, they would probably remind me that the company would meet several times in, the meantime, and that we need not take an appropriation for rolling stock which might or might not be needed three years hence.

That may be a satisfactory mode of argument to the Minister of Finance, but I do not think it would be to any one else. He has not met the suggestion of my hon. friend from Hamilton at all. Has any member of the government any conceivable idea at the present time whether they propose to operate the road in sections or not ?

Yes, I will answer my hon. friend at once. If

the government and the commissioners deem it advantageous to the public that any of those sections should be operated immediately after they are completed, they will be operated.
The policy is, then, not to consider the question immediately, but to consider it by and by ?
You had better wait a year or two before you buy the rolling stock.

You have either to do one thing or the other. You have either to conclude that you will operate it, or to conclude that you will not operate it. If you conclude that you will operate it, you will have to buy rolling stock. In that case, what are you to do with the rolling stock; when you hand the road over to the Grand Trunk Company ? Have the government considered that ? If they do not operate the road, what will happen ? A road which is not operated deteriorates very rapidly. Are the government to have a road four or five years without operation and effective maintenance ? How are they going to maintain the road to a proper standard without having any proper return in the way of traffic ? The Minister of Finance seems to think that the time to consider these matters is by and by. Onq would naturally suppose that the time to consider them is before you make the agreement.

I am obliged to dissent entirely from my hon. friend's position. I see no reason why we should ask parliament to commit itself to details which cannot arise for many months, perhaps for years. When we come to parliament for an expenditure of public money for rolling stock, these questions will be very proper ; and then I have no doubt that the wise government to which I have referred will deal with them.
We will do the best we can with them.
The hon. gentleman is anticipating a government coming into power which would make reckless arrangements, as in the past; but I do not think that is probable.

It is rather amusing to listen to the Fiii a nee Minister after the solemn declaration of the Prime Minister that this scheme commits the government to an expenditure of $13,000,000. When asked about rolling stock, he said that no business man ever looked forward three years.
I did not say that.

I think the Finance Minister said that parliament would meet two or three times in the meantime, and that there Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
would be time enough to provide rolling stock. Is not that right ?
That is a different story.

The inference I draw is that the Finance Minister thinks it is not worth while looking forward to a possible expenditure three or four years from now. The estimate of the Prime Minister was probably arrived at on the same basis.
On what basis was that $560,000,000 estimate arrived at ?
On the basis of the accumulated debt of the Intercolonial Railway.
A very absurd figure.

Not as absurd a figure as many of the figures quoted by my hon. friend the Postmaster General. The increase in the cost of the Intercolonial Railway is exactly what I gave, if the statements of the government are correct. I merely carried out the figures on that basis. But' on this question of rolling stock, let me differ from the Finance Minister when he says that this is the same as a private corporation. An ordinary railway company, looking forward to operating the road for itself, would naturally buy its rolling stock as it goes along. It buys its gravel cars and various other cars for construction purposes ; and as the construction is completed, it turns its construction cars into freight cars, and so gets value for them. An enormous sum of money is expended on construction cars and engines. These engines, if bought by a railway company for its own operation, would be of great value to a new road built in a new country ; but if these cars are supplied to a road which is constructed by a government and which is to be handed'over when completed to a company, we all know as a matter of business experience that the rolling stock becomes practically valueless, because the company leasing that road and operating it will not pay any price for that stock at all. If the government are making no provision for operating this road in sections as it is built, they are overlooking a most material consideration in the cost of this road, and they are committing the country to an enormous addition to the capital cost of this road before it is handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I think that the hon. member for Hamilton is right in asking that the government should give an explanation of what they propose to do with this road as they build it in sections.

While we are discussing the question of the eastern section, might I inquire if the pamphlet which the Prime Minister said was being published giving information in regard to the country which

the eastern section would traverse, is yet completed and ready for distribution ?
Yes, and it will be distributed to-morrow.
Will that contain information as to the practicability, from an engineering point of view, of constructing a railway with 0'4 per cent grade through the province of Quebec.
The pamphlet will be a summary of all the information which is in the library on this subject.
There will be no direct information in the pamphlet from an engineering standpoint ?

I do not think so.
Amendment (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) agreed to, and, section as amended, agreed to.
On section 10,
The commissioners may appoint and employ such engineers (under the chief engineer), and such surveyors and other officers, and also such servants, agents, and workmen, as in their discretion they deem necessary and proper for the execution of the powers and duties vested in them under this Act.
The MINISTER OF JUSTICE moved that section 10 be amended by adding the following words to the end thereof:-The Governor in Council may from time to time designate one of the commissioners to be chairman of the commissioners.

Amendment agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 12,
Any officer or employee appointed by the commissioners who, by virtue of his office or employment, is entrusted with the custody or control of moneys, shall give security in the manner and form, so far as may be, provided by the Act respecting public officers, and in such amount as is fixed by the commissioners.
Section agreed to.
I would like to say a few words in connection with the previous section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman had better move to reconsider section 11.
Mr. PUTTEE moved that section 11 be reconsidered.
Motion agreed to.

I wish to call the attention of the House, in connection with this Section, to the question of the labour that will be employed on the construction of this line. A great deal of this construction work is going to be through a new country with which we are at present not familiar. We have had some experience of this kind of railway construction in Canada before. In 1896, 1897 and 1898 the Crow's Nest pass road was constructed, and in that ease a
good deal of the construction work was similar to what will take place under this Bill. At that time there was a great deal of public sentiment excited, which finally culminated on the loth of January, 1898, in the appointment of a royal commission to examine into all tlie complaints then made and laid before this government. This commission reported on the 30th of April, 1898, and I have before me its report, to which I think it would be well to pay some attention. Although the public money spent on that royal commission then resulted in nothing but a report, we may get some value from that expenditure now by having our attention drawn to the evils which then existed and guarding against their recurrence. Let me just point out some of the scandals that were investigated and which are likely to occur again, if we do not take precautions against them. On page 13, of the report, I find this statement:-
Referring again to that part of the deposition of Mr. Armstrong, he says, that taking into consideration the condition of the men and their ignorance of, and the unsettled condition of the country, it makes it nearly' impossible for them to get any redress by the ordinary course of the law.
It will be remembered that probably the immediate cause of the appointment of the royal commission was the death from negligence of the two men, McDonald and Fraser. The cases were well know at the time but I am not aware that any of the responsible parties were called upon to answer for the deaths of these men. The report says :
Two men, McDonald and Fraser, were taken sick with diphtheria at Mann's camp, about a hundred miles from Macleod. They were seat in open carriage from that place with instructions to be forwarded by the ambulance from Bullhead. They were, however, brought to Crow's Nest pass, about twelve miles east of Bullhead, when they were refused the usual accommodation for patients, and on the same night were driven back to Bullhead. They- were put in an isolated house to await the ambulance. The following day they were conveyed to Sulphur Spring, where they passed the night and in the morning w-ere driven to the end of the track near Pineher Creek. They arrived at that point in the evening and two hours or so latter they died. The only medical attendance they had was that received from Doctor Meade, a private practitioner of Pineher Creek, who was sent for as soon as the end of the track was reached, but was only in time to see them die.
All through this report, it is pointed out ns being proved that men who 'were employed, and who found it necessary to resign rather than put up with the treatment they received, had to tramp all the way back to civilization. Not only that, but as they passed the different camps on the line, they were refused food, the men at work having been instructed not to furnish them with assistance of any kind. Many of these men had to tramp for two or three days from 50 to 150 miles without a bit of food, though

they passed various camps on the way. This was owing to instructions having been given to the camps not to supply any food to men who had been discharged from employment at the end of the line. As these matters are treated in the report I shall not touch on them at any length, but I would press on the government the necessity of taking precautions to see that before this undertaking is commenced, the contractors should be governed by the findings and recommendations contained in this report. One of the most serious grievances was the fees and the transportation charged against the men. This is especially' referred to. A number of the men employed, who were taken from the city of Ottawa and across the river at Hull, gave evidence on this score. The commissioners submit a table showing that, after the various fees and transportation charges were deducted from their pay, men who worked twelve months continually, and allowing $5 per month for personal expenses, would have $5.10 coming to them. If they had only worked nine months, when they arrived at Ottawa they were $22.40 cents in the debt of the company. This was actually the case in one matter referred to, where 80 employees joined together and entered a suit against one of the sub-contractors, and I believe got judgment but the case was appealed, and being unable to stay and follow up the appeal, these men had to accept from the contractor transportation back to Ottawa and $5 to buy food on the way back, which was a poor recompense for the work they put in.
I just wish to place before you some of the general grievances which the commission found had been proved and the recommendations of the commission :
First the non-compliance on the pant of the company and the contractors with the terms of the agreement, more particularly to the end of September.
That is a matter which could be arranged for with a little forethought.
2.	The lack of proper attendance to the men in several instances when reaching Maclecd.
3.	The forcing of men to sleep in the open air in some instances without blankets on the hare ground, or in cold and filthy houses, box cars or boarding cars, not being fit to keep men in for any length of time.
4.	The lack of proper washing accommodation and more particularly on the works in some of the contractors' camps, which besides not being properly attended to, because full of vermin and were filthy inside and outside, and had no or not sufficient light, ventilation or proper shelter.
5.	The keeping of men under tents until the beginning of January without stoves.
6.	The feeding of the men in some instances, and without good reason, with frozen provisions.
7.	The threatening of the men with discharge if they should make complaints or representations.
8.	The charging of mail fees against their consent.

9.	The loss of time during which they were kept idle either after they had reached Macleod, or after they had begun work, whether due to bad weather or to causes uncontrollable by the men, or whether the employer had no work for the time being.
And the great grievanpe,-
10.	The charging of fare to Macleod and from Macleod to the works, and board, even for meals which the men did not get, and the refusal to recognize the alleged right of the men to he returned home free or at reduced rates after a certain time as represented by the agents.
These that I am reading are general grievances which, the commission say the evidence lias fairly established :
14.	The refusal of meals to sick persons and the determination of sub-officials to send them to work, notwithstanding their sickness, and in some instances discharging them.
15.	The low rate of wage which left the men in the position of being scarcely able to meet their expenses and charges from the time they left home bo the date of return, many of them never getting out of debt to the company and being compelled to walk the whole distance home, sometimes nearly 2,250 miles, and in all cases destitute and exposed to all sorts of hardships.
Tlie commission, after investigation, have stated these as facts. I happen to know them to bo so of my own knowledge. I have seen men passing through Winnipeg, even from as far west as the Rocky mount-1 a ins who had come on foot and intended to go east on foot. It was the policy of the government in the case of this construction that Canadians should be employed as far as possible. Canadians were employed, some of them coming from as far east as Halifax, most of them from Quebec and Ontario, including many from tlie city of Ottawa and the city of Hull. And, during that winter, I saw many men who had to tramp all the way from the west and intended going east from Winnipeg, undertaking to get home by tramping, after having worked for months and having left tlie company even poorer than when they entered its service. Now, some of the recommendations of this commission, it seems to me, are particularly applicable at this time; and not only should they be carefully considered. but some action should be based upon them. The commissioners say :
We also found that the payment by time cheques, bank cheques, and the giving of time records, caused the men great loss of time and money.
This, of course, is one of the great evils of railway construetibn. Time checks are given to men leaving the employment of the company, these checks being payable at the headquarters of the company and only on some particular day. The result is that the men have to take a reduction on the checks from some store or from people who make a business of cashing the checks at a discount; or these checks may be carried

by the men in their pockets and never cashed at all. I believe, that, as a matter of fact, construction companies on undertakings of this kind do make a very large percentage of profit in uncashed time checks:
Although the sleeping accommodation may be somewhat improved since the commencement of construction, yet as far as we are aware the grounds of complaint forming the subject of this inquiry still exist.
This was at the end of the winter, that is why the point is noted :
That employment agents in future be subject to government regulation, and a general system adapted to ascertain the physical condition and fitness of the men seeking employment.
That regulations be adopted- to protect employers from imposition by the men, by assuming false names, of making improper use of transportation granted them, cheating or defrauding employees whilst under employment, &c.
That general or special rules, according to the nature of the work or the distances, be fixed as to fare, food, cost of supplies, washing and sleeping accommodation, working days, rale of wages, medical attendance, hospitals, &c., and such other regulations as would protect the honest labourer against imposition and his own improvidence.
That the company, or chief employer, be responsible directly and indirectly for the reasonably prompt payment for all wages earned on the construction of the work.
' That wherever practicable there would be greater satisfaction generally if the men's wages are paid at shorter intervals than at present prevail. The terms of the contract with the men should be carefully supervised before the engagement is completed. The scale of wages on the present work should be at least from $2 to $2.50 per day for labourers and board from $4 to $5 per week.
That no liquor should be allowed to he sold on or near works of this kind.
That is an important point ; and I would suggest that this undertaking, which is to be such a large one, will be certain to involve us in dealing with these questions before the thousands of men employed on it have finished their work. It should be laid down as a rule that all wages should be paid weekly. I conceive that there is no practical objection to this proposal. Large companies do make objection, because it suits them to pay by time cheeks, and to have only one ' cashing-in day,' as they call it, each month, holding back always fourteen days' pay. But I believe it would be practical, and woidd certainly be a great benefit, to insist on weekly pay throughout this work. The commissioners reported also :
That independent government officials be appointed with certain magisterial powers permitting them to settle on the spot all difficulties and complaints arising between employers and employees and to see the proper execution of the rules and regulations in force.
That is a very important recommendation and has a bearing on the suggestion that
there should be weekly pay days. It is a custom with large contractors to object to frequent pay days because they say, it is impossible to get a considerable portion of the men to work after such pay days. If this recommendation were carried out, it would overcome that objection altogether. The recommendation is that no liquor be allowed to be sold on or near works of this kind. The next recommendation is this :
That the above suggestions apply to all public works wherever the government intervenes directly or indirectly and as far as possible to the work in question.
The commission would have this apply to all works in which the government is interested directly or indirectly. I take it that, in regard to this proposed work, or over a large portion of it, the government would he directly interested ; and on the whole line, from east to west, it might properly be said that the government is interested directly. At all events, there is no part in which it is not Indirectly interested, because on the whole line it guarantees the bonds. If the system of time-check payment is allowed there should be some new method altogether to ensure that the men receiving these checks shall be able to cash them at other than the one place specified by the company. It seems to me that it would not be out of the way to suggest that the government officers in any town should have the power, or should even have the duty imposed upon them to cash these time-checks. For instance, where there is a customs officer, it seems to me these checks could be cashed, and if necessary, the company could be charged five per cent to discourage the practice of giving time-cheeks instead of wages to the men leaving their employment. This report of that commission on the Crow's Nest Pass work was a good report. At that time, it was of no practical use, because too late in the history of the construction of that work. But it should be studied and should be availed of, and, as far as possible, followed out now, 'before the actual contracts or sub-contracts are let.
There is also one other matter that might lie referred to in this connection, and it is one concerning which there has already been some complaint.
All through this country, more especially perhaps in the west, it has become a frequent practice of construction companies to bring in American civil engineers. That has loing been a source of grievous complaint so far as the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned, and I believe that their, officials make it a practice each season to bring over from the United States classes from the various colleges and educational institutions there, and give them work for experience, and they go back into the United States at the end of the season. At the same time our civil engineers are idle, our own engineering students who are graduated from

^universities in this country, are in nearly every case forced to seek employment in the United States. I believe it is a matter of fact that the graduating classes of this country, go over almost in a body across the line to obtain employment in their calling for which we have educated them. On the surveys that are being made at the present time west and north of Lake Superior, the complaint is already being made that the work is done almost entirely by American civil engineers. Seeing that this contract is a public one made by the government of Canada, we are bound to take the responsibility for this; at all events, it appears to me that the matter could be remedied and should be at this time.

I was not present when my hon. friend began his argument, and X do not know if he has concluded it with an amendment. I agree with everything he has said with regard to the necessity of employing engineers of our own country. As to the pay of the workmen, I think it is a rule that should extend to all government employees who do work for which they receive a small salary. The advantage of that custom, in the city of Montreal for example, would be considerable to those who deal with the labourers employed by the government, canal men and others, because they would get paid in cash, as a rule, for everything that these men buy, they would run no risk of losing, and they could sell what the workman has to buy at a cheaper price. But when you consider the advantage it would be to the work-1 ingmen themselves, I do not see how the government can avoid adopting the suggestion of my hon. friend from Winnipeg and amending clause 11 so as to provide for weekly payments. As a rule the workingman who is paid now at longer intervals has to deal with the same man, and he lias to pay an excessive price for the necessaries of life. He has to buy on credit, whereas if be were paid weekly he would be able to purchase for cash, he would be able to purchase where he pleased and get his articles both cheaper and better. So weekly payments would be an advantage not only for the dealer but for the workingman himself, and I hope the government will adopt the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee). On government works where the contractor frequently keeps a store and deals with the workingmen, weekly payments would be particularly advantageous to them. That is a suggestion often made to me by working associations in Montreal, who desire to see weekly payments incorporated in the law. If it is necessary make it fifteen days-as a rule government employees are not paid every fifteen days, at least that is the case on the canals. I know that the working associations in the city of Montreal are unanimous in favour of weekly payments.

and I think the government ought to adopt this suggestion and incorporate it in clause 11, otherwise we will have a renewal of those abuses which have invariably arisen on the constuction of railways in this country.
With respect to the civil engineers, I think the suggestion of my hon. friend from Winnipeg should receive the approval of the government. I do not know how they are situated in the west, but in the city of Montreal I know that the University of McGill turns out very competent engineers. In Laval University they have an affiliated polytechnic school, as my right hon. friend knows, and they are erecting a new building for that purpose. They turn out first-class engineers, who very often have to go to the United States where they are gladly received and given employment. Now, since this whole scheme is a patriotic one, why not insert in this clause 11 a provision that the commissioners shall employ only Canadian engineers on this railway ? If such a clause were put in I am sure it would have a very beneficial effect. But I am sorry to see that amendments which have been proposed of a very serious character this evening are left in abeyance, or treated as one was a moment ago by the acting Minister of Railways and Canals in a jocose manner.
I was In dead earnest.

I hope my hon. friend will be more serious in regard to this amendment. Let us put an amendment im clause 11 calling for the weekly payment of the workingmen. That will be of great advantage to them, it will protect them, and it will also protect the dealers.
Protect them from what ?
Is it the Minister of Labour who is asking that question ? Did not the Minister of Labour listen to what I said a moment ago, and what was much better said by the hon. member for Winnipeg ?

Would the hon. gentleman be good enough, after he has done abusing me, to say what protection the workingmen would get from weekly payments ?
Mr, MONK. I have never, since I have brought matters of interest to the workingmen to the attention of the Minister of Labour, received the slightest assistance. Now the Minister of Labour remembers how be treated the workingmen of Cartierville.
I know what a friend the hon. gentleman was, what a humbug he was in that affair.

He remembers that he -would not protect these three workingmen who had been abused by a government contractor. Now the Minister of Labour asks me how

labouring men would be protected by weekly payments. Well, I may tell him that there are hundreds of labour organizations in the city of Montreal who have asked for weekly payments. I will tell him that the labouring man who is paid every week is not the slave of the dealer for the necessaries of life ; he has the cash in Ills hands, and he is able to go around and choose among the stores the best things for his family, he can buy them at cash price, and thereby he escapes from the thraldom of the dealer. The Minister of Labour did not know jtliat. Why, when this Bill was brought into the House, Mr. Darlington, who represents one of the labour organizations of Montreal, came to me and asked me to see that weekly payments should be made to the labouring men. The Minister of Labour, who has been two or three years in office, rises, when I speak of weekly payments, and wants to know if they are going to be of any use to the workingmen.

The hon. gentleman should not put words into my mouth that I did not use. The hon. gentleman said that if the contract called for payment by the week we could protect the workingmen in respect to his wages. I asked him if he would explain what protection he alluded to. I do not say that payment by the week would not be to the benefit of the workingman. I would remind the hon. gentleman that when this government took office we found that the government was not in the habit of paying the civil service at less frequent intervals than a whole month.
You pay them every month ?

When we took office the practice of our predecessors was to pay monthly and we have modified that practice, at all events, as far as my department is concerned and I think other departments to the extent of paying fortnightly. Throughout the whole Post Office Department we have improved upon the practice we found in force when we took office and those engaged in the service are paid fortnightly. I asked my hon. friend in all humility to explain what he meant by saying that weekly payments would protect them. I thought when he said 1 protection ' that he meant that the workman might run a less risk of losing his wage, the more frequently he was paid the less financial risk he would run. If I had understood that he used the term in that sense I would have explained to him that the contract provides ample protection in so far as payment is concerned though perhaps the question of frequency is not covered. Section 40 provides that :
The company shall, before being entitled to the guarantee provided by this agreement, furnish evidence, satisfactorily to the government, that all just claims of contractors and for materials, wages and supplies, and all just
claims against contractors and sub-contractors for materials, wages and supplies entering into and supplied for the construction of the railway have been duly paid.
So flint under that clause in so far as getting his pay is concerned

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That only applies to the western section.

The company cannot get the guarantee until the wages are paid. As far as these concessions are concerned the government would he the contractor and the government will provide in the contract it makes for the construction of this section for the payment of the workingmen.
My hon. friend asked me in what way weekly payment would protect the workingman.
The hon. gentleman used the word ' protection ' and I asked him to kindly explain what he meant.

I meant the protection which has been advocated by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) and advocated by me-protection in this sense that if the payment is more extended the workingman becomes a prey of the contractor and becomes to a certain extent his slave.
There is no doubt about that.

But my hon. friend had something else in view. He meant protection as far as the working man being secured in his wages is concerned and lie referred to section 40 of the contract, but, as a distinguished lawyer, I am quite sure that he will readily appreciate that this clause 40 of the contract applies only to the western part of the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme. Is there anything in the contracts which protects the workingman on the eastern section ?
Surely the government, when it prepares its contract, will be responsible for the payment of wages and it will put in proper safeguards.
My hon. friend knows perfectly well that the government will not be responsible for wages ?
It will not ?
It is not going to give contracts.
The government will make a stipulation in regard to wages.
We shall see that the wages are paid by the contractors.

The very painful experience that I have had with the hon. Minister of Labour has led me to the conclusion that he will not protect the workingman against the contractor. That is the experience in connection with the building at Nelson where $1,200 was taken from three workingmen.

That is not the ease. The case, if I remember rightly was, that the hon. gentleman had three clients who came to him with their claims. He told them that they had perfectly valid claims, that the debtors were perfectly solvent and after they put the case into the hands of my hon. friend, although there was no doubt whatever according to his advice that they would recover, for some reason he preferred not to recover these moneys for his unfortunate clients, but, he has got a grievance nominally against the government. He has assured them that there is no question as to their legal rights and .vet he will not take steps to recover these claims for his clients. I think the hon. gentleman has neglected his duty.

I never would have imagined that the hon. Postmaster General had such a small opinion of me as to think that I would choose among my electors who have been ill-treated by him clients to make money out of. I never take a case from among my constituents. I do not know whether it is a rule adopted by my hon. friend, but it is a rule that has been followed in Jacques Cartier by lawyers since the time Mr. Laflamme was Minister of Justice in the same cabinet as that of which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was a member. There is a tradition in Jacques Cartier that the person representing the constituency, being a lawyer, will not take a case in order to make money out of his constituents.
The hon. gentleman told us in the House that these men were his clients.

On the contrary, I denied that I had any legal relations with these men. I brought the oase to the attention of the department as their representative. I appealed to the hon. Minister of Labour to protect them and the Department of Labour had some understanding with the Department of Public Works
That is not correct.
Although the hon. Minister of Labour, I must say, disclaimed all responsibility by saying that he had been absent at the time.
I did not disclaim it at all.

I therefore forgive him to a certain extent, although I cannot forgive Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
him now. But, in this case, there is no doubt that the contractors, Messrs, Lemoine, were paid $1,200 which belonged to these three workingmen and the only recourse they had was the recourse that I repeatedly suggested. The hon. Minister of Labour says that the recourse of law was open to them but I told him then as I tell him now that we pay $40,000 a year to maintain his Department of Labour to save the workingmen from the misfortune of falling into the hands of men who will not meet their obligations.

I commiserate with them under the circumstances because it appears that these unfortunate clients appealed to him to exercise that great legal acumen of his to recover their rights and he neglected to recover their rights.
In a certain sense I look upon all my constituents as my clients. In the county of Jacques Cartier if the member happens to be a lawyer he takes no clients from among his constituents.
In this ease my hon. friend said that they were his clients.
My hon. friend has not referred to the report.
I remember quite well.
My hon. friend is not very correct in a great many cases. However, we will leave that case aside. It is still open, the government has still contracts with Messrs. Lemoine.
The hon. gentleman is still their counsel too ; it is still in his power to help them.
After I have stated to the Minister of Labour that these gentlemen are not my clients, he has no right to contradict me.
Neither do I think that the hon. gentleman has a right to misrepresent me. He knows quite well that it was not through me that these workmen were not paid.
I know that my hon. friend tried to escape responsibility by stating that he was absent.
I was many thousands of miles away, but I never once stated that I was absent. The hon. gentleman was good enough to state that for me, and to say that I was not personally responsible.
Might I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we come back to the question before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I am drawing an analogy as to the conduct of the government. I am proceeding by exemplification.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is sufficient to use it as an illustration.
Do you hold that I cannot give as an example the treatment meted out to three workmen by the government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think you can, but I think both of you went beyond that.
I was led into the discussion by the Minister of Dabour.
Well go on with the Grand Trunk Bill now.
I am sure the Minister of Labour will be glad when I abandon the question of the three workmen of Cartier-ville.
That's a raw spot.

Some provision ought to be made in regard to the engineers, and in this respect I appeal particularly to the Prime Minister. I do not refer especially to McGill, because the engineering course in McGill has already a very high reputation. We have in Laval university of Montreal a new polyteclmical school, and we have young men who are filling a great void which has existed in our province. My right lion, friend knows that classical studies are paid much attention to in the province of Quebec, and that technical studies have to some extent not attained prominence in the past. That Laval scientific school has been opened under able teachers, and I think we should encourage its students. A provision in this Bill enjoining the government as far as possible to give the preference to Canadian engineers would be very popular ; much more popular than the preamble of the Bill, which speaks of the work as a grand national undertaking. We should have a national enactment in the Bill to protect our workingmen, and to protect our young men who are studying engineering. The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) is a most useful one.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Probably the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) thought it was unnecessary to have a prepared amendment in this direction, as no doubt he believed that the Minister of Labour would accept his suggestion. If it is not accepted by the Minister of Labour, then the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) should move to amend section II, so that Canadian surveyors, engineers, and workingmen should be employed. Not only that, but he should move to provide that these employees should be paid their wages weekly. Some years ago the manufacturers of Ontario paid their men once a month, but it was found that this was inconvenient to labouring men with large families who
had to run into debt for their supplies, and on the insistence of the workingmen, the manufacturers paid fortnightly, and latterlyi they have been paying weekly. In a project of this magnitude the government ought to make provision that all the employees should be paid their wages weekly. It is as easy for the contractors to pay weekly as monthly, and it would add to the wages of the men at least 10 per cent if this were done. In my town there are 700 or 800 men employed, and in Toronto there are thousands and thousands of workingmen, and they are all paid weekly. Why should not the government adopt that system ? The Minister of Labour says that he has changed from monthly to fortnightly payments in his department, but he should go one better and pay his employees weekly. Every civil servant should draw his wages weekly the same as every other labourer in the country. If that were done the civil servants would not have to go to brokers to discount their salary checks weeks in advance in order to get food for their families. I understand that there are brokers on Sparks street in the city here, making a large amount out of the civil servants by discounting their checks in this way. The Minister of Labour ought to see to it, that every governfinent employee should receive his pay once a week.
They don't want it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They don't want it ?
Not all of them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Leave it to the civil servants themselves and you will find out.
My deputy told me that when we sent out the fortnightly checks, a good many preferred the old plan, but we adhered to the fortnightly system.
Is there much kick now about taking the checks fortnightly ?
My deputy informed me that there was an objection from some of the officers of my department.

The tendency to-day is to pay workmen more frequently than in the past, and I think we should respond to that sentiment. I have not myself had my attention called to the question of weekly payments, but I know that as respects a large portion of workingmen in my own province, we legislated to give them fortnightly payments. What may be a good system in the city may not be necessarily equally applicable to the rural sections. I am not sure that up amongst those muskegs and jackpines, it would be so important for a man to have

his money every Saturday night, 'as it would be in the city of Toronto. In regard to the engineering side of the question, I am sorry my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has so little faith in the young engineers of Laval and McGill. He seems to think they will not be employed unless we force their employment by an Act of parliament. I have faith enough in these young men to believe that they will be employed on their merits, that a preference will be given to them, and that there is no need of an Act of parliament to force them on an unwilling company or contractors. You need no legislation, at any rate as respects this government, to induce the employment of Canadians in preference to others. You might push that principle too far. My hon. friend from Winnipeg, under a severe rule, might find himself excluded from representing a constituency in Canada, as he is only recently a Canadian.
I object to that.

I am referring to what might happen if we excluded a man who comes from another part of the empire, which we do not wish to do. However, there is no doubt that wherever Canadian engineers of standing are available, they will receive employment, and there will be no need of an Act of parliament for that purpose.

I think if the minister will look a little further into this matter, he will see that there is need of some encouragement. In the railway construction which has taken place in Canada in the last few years, Canadian engineers have been discriminated against by construction companies. This matter, I believe, has already been brought to the attention of the ministers. Large numbers of young men are being brought into Canada from colleges and universities in the United States to take a part of their course on our railroads, obtaining the experience that should be given to our own students. If the minister will look at the record of one of the graduating classes in the city of Toronto last year, he will find that fourteen graduated and fourteen left for the United States the following week. There must be, then, some means of encouraging our own people. I do not believe that our Canadian people in any branch of life need absolute protection, or that other people should be barred out completely. Rut in our great corporations the principal positions are held by citizens of the United States ; and when they have plums to give out, they do as a matter of fact give to young men from the other side of the line these plums which legitimately belong to our own people.
Referring to the question of what is the benefit of a weekly wage, it makes a great difference how much a salary is how often you get it. A large salary can very easily be paid in four quarterly instal-Hon. Mrs FIELDING.
ments ; but a salary of $1 or $1.50 a day is a very different thing paid every week from what it is if it is paid once a month, with two weeks held back to give a lever to the employer, and with the statement that if you leave the service those two weeks' salary will be payable only at the head quarters of the company, which, in the case of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, was 2,000 miles from the place where the check was issued. The great benefit of the weekly wage system in construction work of this kind would be that it would do away with the time-check system. Some of these time-checks are never paid. In the case of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, time-checks were sent back to Winnipeg from as far as Sault Ste. Marie, which were utterly useless, but indicated the great hardship the men had suffered who had left that work and tramped away. I did not move an amendment to this section, because I could not see that any fragmentary amendment I could put together would meet the case. I did not wish to have any amendment voted down. My object was to call the attention of the responsible officers to the report of the Crow's Nest Pass commission. That report was made by three gentlemen who had given three or four months of their time and attention to an inquiry into a similar matter to that which is under discussion. They had examined two or three hundred witnesses. They had sat in the mountains, in the centre of the country, in Ottawa and in Montreal. They had heard the men who employed the labour, the employment agents, the men on the work, the men who had tramped back to the east without money, sometimes even without boots ; and after devoting their attention for three or four months to this matter, it seemed to me that their report would be far more valuable than any summary made by myself and moved as an amendment at the present time. I submit that that report should be conned over very carefully by members of the government or their officers who are competent and prepared to formulate either clauses or a schedule that would fit the case, to be included either in this Bill or in the contract.

The hon. member for Winnipeg in the first part of his remarks drew attention to that portion of the report in the Crow's Nest Pass Railway referring to the health of the employees. I may state that the year after that report this parliament passed an Act known as the Public Health Act, which has been administered since that time in regard to all public works and railway construction in Canada, and regulations and rules under that Act have been adopted by Order in Council. A copy of these rules and regulations was placed on the Table of- this House in 1900, and they have been faithfully and effectively carried out since that time.
Who is the employee who lias charge of the carrying out of the Publ-lic Health Act ?
The inspector is Mr. Fisher.

I am aware that the recommendations in regard to health have been taken note of by the quarantine officers and that a great deal of good has resulted from the regulations drawn up by the officer in charge of that Act. That strengthens my argument that the other regulations of the commission could very well be taken up, and probably the rules and regulations laid down in the Department of Agriculture could be attached to the rules and regulations applying to other matters and grievances that have not so far been given any force at all. The matters of the pay, the transportation, and the general care of the men should not be left absolutely at the mercy of the camp bosses and sub-contractors. In bringing this matter before the government, it was my hope to accomplish something, not to embarrass them at all. It seems to me that it should be a valuable suggestion at this time, that if something is not done there will be abuses, there will be agitation, and probably royal commissions, who will report as usual after the fact, when the report is simply useful for reading, and that is all.
What reports has the hon. minister received since 1900 with respect to the Health Act ?
There is a report made every year, which is embodied in the report of the Department of Agriculture, which is laid on the Table.
How does it work out

It works out in this way. The regulations, which were laid on the Table in the year 1000. require certain accommodation for working people on public works. They required that medical attendance shall be available and hospital accommodations where cases can be taken in and be treated. The inspector's duty is to see that the regulations are carried out. and lie makes a tour at least, once a year through every public work in the country.
Only once a year ?
At least once a year. In addition, if anything occurs to indicate that the work is not being properly conducted, he goes and investigates.
Has he made any report about infringement of the law ?
He makes reports from time to time about the work to Dr. Montizambert.
Who is the gentleman ?
Sir. C. A. Fisher.

I am in thorough accord with the request of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), and I have had probably more experience in matters of this kind than most hon. members. While I think it important that a system of weekly payment should be established, or at least payments every half month, there is another matter in this connection which I think of great importance. In the construction of a railway, hundreds of miles away from the centres of population, men will have to be provided no doubt by the contractors with goods, and it is just as Important not only to see that tiie men are paid frequently but that, when they have to buy from the contractors' stores, they are dealt with fairly in the matter of quality and price. I would suggest that the Minister of Labour or the [DOT]government should undertake to arrange that the workmen on this great railway shall be paid fortnightly and shall not be swindled in quality of price when they buy from the contractors.

I think that the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) deserves great credit for having brought this matter to the attention of the government. Section 40, which the Postmaster General has quoted. does not go far enough to remedy the grievance of which the hon. member for Winnipeg complains. IVe all remember quite well that in the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, the men had to endure many hardships and some of them lost their lives. Advantage was taken of the men by the foremen and others personally interested on behalf of the contractor, and there is no provision at all made here against grievances of that character. There are good foremen on construction work and others again who are inclined to be arbitrary, and think they are performing their duties best when acting very arbitraily towards those employed under them. The government should provide some remedy for the workmen who have grievances of that character. Again it is well known that there are employment agencies which take advantage of the labourers who seek employment on the contraction of railways. Some provision should be made for the protection of the labourers against these employment bureaus. I am glad to notice that, according to the statement of the Minister of Agriculture, the Public Works Health Act provides for better accommodation for these labourers. In the case of the Crow's Nest Pass, that was a serious grievance, but I was very sorry to hear the hon. gentleman say that inspector only visits the works once a year. It would require more frequent inspection to see that the Act is properly carried out. I have sim-



ply drawn the attention of tlie government to some of these things that I think very important to those engaged on construction work. If they were employed on construction work in the neighbourhood of Oltawa, there would be no great hardships, but out in the wilderness the case is different. It has been said many times that the Canadian Pacific Railway are responsible for the suffering of these men at Crow's Nest Pass. I understand that Mr. Haney had that contract. He is a very respectable mau and extensive contractor. He has had very large contracts on the ' Soo ' canal in partnership with the late Mr. Hugh Ryan, and is a man from who the public would naturally expect fair treatment to the men lie employed. I have heard it frequently said that the Canadian Pacific Railway are entirely responsible for what took place at the Crow's Nest Pass, and I think it is oily fair to that company to ,say that it was not responsible, but, that it was the contractors who were really to blame. I hope that nothing of the kind will occur in connection with this new railway, but that the government will see that the men are properly treated. With respect to time checks and the cashing of these checks, that is a grievance on all new railway work. We know, that there are many stakemen who go on a railway that is being constructed and who will not work the required time. They will work a certain period and before the time comes to receive their pay, they leave the service and get their cheeks discounted by persons who make a considerable amount of money by shaving them. I would ask the lion. Minister of Agriculture how long the inspector remains when he is visiting a public work to see that the Public Works Health Act is complied with.

1 think perhaps the hon. gentleman did not quite comprehend the duties of the general inspector. His duty is to go around the different public works, under the operation of the Act, and see that the rules and regulations passed by Order in Council are enforced, but one of these rules requires that there shall be a medical man on every such public work, for every 500 employees, and he must visit the work every ten days at least. The works are thus really visited at least once every ten days, although the inspector might not very often visit any particular work. The employees on all these works know that certain rules and regulations have to be carried out, and, at any time, they have it in their power to make complaint, first, to the local inspector. and then, if they choose, to the general inspector to see that the regulations are properly carried out. Speaking from memory, I think there are only two or three instances in which complaints have been made to the department of the rules not being carried out. The general inspector immediately visited the works to see that the Mr. INGRAM.
regulations were enforced. The local inspection is carried on all the time, as provided for by the rules and regulations.
I presume that the hon. minister's report contains the report of the medical officer visiting the works from time to time.

The report is that of the general inspector, and in it reference is made to the different works visited and the way in which the regulations are carried out. The general inspector examines the local inspectors' reports, but I do not think the report contains the report of any local inspector.
I desire, in one word to call attention to the injustice suffered by the men in many cases in the high prices charged for supplies of food, clothing, &c., for their use.
Of course, the hon. gentleman understands that the inspector of public health has nothing to do with that.

Of course, I am drawing the attention of the government generally to this point, and I think steps should be taken to remedy this evil. But we shall have another opportunity of expressing our views more fully on this important aspect of the question.
Section 11 agreed to.
Section 12 agreed to.

I think it well to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to that, and he might consider the advisability of referring the parties to the Railway Act for compensation, or providing some machinery.

The Bill and resolution with respect to the Civil Service Act, standing in my name, I desire to change. I move, therefore, that these orders, No. 22 and No. 24, be discharged. I purpose reintroducing them with certain changes.
Are these changes on the lines suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) ?
That will appear when the Bill is introduced. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) will then have better authority than my description for any conclusion he may draw.
